episodes.title: Mark Kendall Thinks A Good Joke Can Help Us Change Our Communities.
episodes.summary: Atlanta comedian and filmmaker Mark Kendall describes how a Comedy Central summer program built by Chris Rock put him in the writers' rooms of The Daily Show and The Colbert Report. He talks about using comedy on public issues with partners such as the Atlanta Regional Commission (affordable housing), Fair Count (redistricting), Open Buffalo, and PBS's Independent Lens (Black Sustainability History), and about his touring solo show The Magic Negro and Other Blackness.
ideas: Good comedy needs a clear point of view and something the comedian cares about
Laughter is a momentary act of shared agreement
Hyperlocal specificity can make material feel universal

episodes.title: Sierra Leone Believes Poetry Is Essential Civic Infrastructure: Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two of the conversation with Dayton poet laureate Sierra Leone. She reads her poem responding to Carolyn Crump's quilt portrait of Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson, describes The Belonging Project, a verbatim-theater work built from listening sessions with about 130 Dayton residents, and shares a poem born of a visit to the Equal Justice Initiative's Legacy Sites in Montgomery.
ideas: Poetry and democracy both ask questions each generation must answer
Poets lift up the parts of the story that fall to the ground
Residents' own stories become theater and community dialogue in The Belonging Project

episodes.title: Sierra Leone Believes Poetry Is Essential Civic Infrastructure: Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one of the conversation with Dayton poet laureate Sierra Leone, the Kettering Foundation's inaugural Democracy and the Arts artist in residence. She traces her path from 'healing producer' to 'creative catalyst' to 'culture keeper,' and describes poetry living in schools, galleries, theaters and public squares, including her tribute to Dayton artist Willis 'Bing' Davis.
ideas: Presence is a creative discipline
Poetry can become civic infrastructure
Belonging is something a community makes together

episodes.title: Liz Lerman Part 2:  What Can Witches Teach us About Art & Social Change
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: Part two with choreographer Liz Lerman centers on Wicked Bodies, her intergenerational performance work about witches, and asks why some knowledge is honored, some erased and some criminalized. The conversation turns to cultural humility, aesthetic equity and how outside artists can enter a community as accountable partners.
ideas: Every culture has its witches: knowledge celebrated, erased or criminalized
Cultural humility and aesthetic equity for artists entering communities
No singular stories: work built through shared inquiry and consent
orgs: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts

episodes.title: Liz Lerman Part 1: The Critical, the Horizontal, & the Heretic's Path
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: Choreographer Liz Lerman talks about her early years, her 'heretic's path,' the Critical Response Process, and 'the horizontal,' a way of sharing leadership and expertise in a room or community without giving them up. It is the third episode in a four-part look at how outside artists can partner with communities.
ideas: The Horizontal: sharing leadership and expertise without disappearing
Critical Response: feedback built on curiosity, consent and respect
The Heretic's Path: challenging systems while staying in relationship
orgs: California State Summer School for the Arts

episodes.title: Eric Gottesman Asks: Whose Questions Get Asked -Whose Story is Told?
episodes.summary: Artist Eric Gottesman traces his path from documentary photographer in Ethiopia to collaborative image-maker with AIDS-affected communities in Addis Ababa, and on to co-founding For Freedoms, which uses billboards, artist-led town halls and a reimagining of Rockwell's Four Freedoms to spark civic discourse. He describes new work on a 'composite nation' drawn from Frederick Douglass.
ideas: Asking the right question often matters more than delivering the right answer
No one makes art alone
A 'composite nation' built from multiplicity rather than a single official story
approaches: Artists in politics and running for office
orgs: Center for Documentary Studies at Duke University
Corcoran School of the Arts & Design

episodes.title: Can Art Build Trust & Love Between Separated Communities?
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: A reprise of Kathi Bentley's story of Love at the River's Edge, a 2019 Shakespeare in the Streets production of As You Like It that joined rural, largely white Brussels, Illinois with the predominantly Black communities of Normandy and Pagedale, Missouri. Casts and audiences crossed the Mississippi by bus and ferry, and strangers became castmates and friends.
ideas: Collective creation can change settled worldviews
Bridges between communities are built when people come to love each other
Leadership that steps back grows community ownership

episodes.title: Tricia Rose Burt - This Is No Time For Artists to Be Timid!
episodes.summary: Moth storyteller and podcaster Tricia Rose Burt tells how she left a corporate communications career at Fidelity and Harvard Business School, moved to an artist's studio in Ireland for what became four years, and built a creative life. She shares what musicians and makers told her about fear and her 10-point manifesto for getting unstuck.
ideas: The cost of staying is as real as the cost of going
Fear never goes away; you get better at using it
Practicality is overrated and constraints are opportunities

episodes.title: Who Tells America's Story?
episodes.summary: A solo episode on the White House's July 4, 2026 report accusing the Smithsonian's National Museum of American History of 'ideological capture,' a follow-up executive order, and stalled board appointments. Drawing on work in Serbia, Cambodia, Northern Ireland and Watts, Bill argues that authoritarian movements target culture first because stories shape what people believe is possible.
ideas: A report, an executive order and a board stall are one strategy for controlling the national story
Authoritarian movements go after imagination first
Democracy is a creative practice rehearsed in museums, story circles and theater

episodes.title: Why Are Dopamine, Synapsis', & the Prefrontal Cortex Critical to Art & Social Change?
episodes.summary: After time with Breaking Ice's theater-based DEI work in St. Louis, Bill shares a layperson's tour of neuroscience: dopamine, synapses and the prefrontal cortex, and what they suggest about empathy, storytelling and the human struggle with difference. He is clear that brain science is no substitute for the moral work of anti-racism.
ideas: Neuroscience can help explain the human struggle with difference
Empathy is a fundamental part of humanity that artists can harness
Art can rewire how we think about ourselves and each other

episodes.title: Can Outside Activist Artists Make a Difference in Your Community?
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: Bill, Alice Lovelace and Barbara Schaffer Bacon ask whether artists from outside a community can make a lasting difference. Through stories from Serbia, Atlanta, Ohio and rural Georgia, they discuss local leadership, the outsider as catalyst or lightning rod, and measuring success by the relationships and capacity left behind.
ideas: Local knowledge and leadership must shape the work from the start
An outsider can sometimes raise what locals cannot safely say
Success is the relationships, skills and power that remain after the artist leaves

episodes.title: Ken Grossinger Believes Art is Essential to Effective Organizing
series: Block, Bridge, Build: Stories of Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers
episodes.summary: Labor strategist Ken Grossinger explains how marrying an artist showed him the gap in organizing: policy wins fade, but stories and art last. Drawing on his book Art Works, he describes collaborations between artists and organizers, from a museum exhibit in Louisville to musicians protecting Alaska's Bristol Bay.
ideas: Organizers can't work effectively without culture
Art drives the narrative shifts effective organizing depends on
Artists and organizers each need to learn the other's strategy

episodes.title: Effective Community Arts Practice - Should Activist Artists Prioritize Safety or Bravery
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: Bill, Alice Lovelace and Barbara Schaffer Bacon ask whether artists should prioritize safety or bravery now. Recalling the 1980s culture wars and NEA grant fights, they discuss creative courage, the ecosystems of support that make it possible, and the tools artists bring to uncertain times.
ideas: Creative courage takes many forms, not only public protest
Healthy cultural ecosystems make courage possible
Artists' everyday skills are tools society needs now

episodes.title: What Makes a Healthy Art and Social Change Ecosystem?
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: Bill, Alice Lovelace and Barbara Schaffer Bacon ask what makes a healthy art and social change ecosystem. They argue that cultural health doesn't happen by accident, isn't defined by economic development, and depends on connecting artists with public health, education, environmental justice and youth development.
ideas: Healthy arts ecosystems don't happen by accident
Cultural health is not the same as economic development
Strong ecosystems reach well beyond the arts into other sectors

episodes.title: Ariel Fristoe: -Theater as a Civic Commons
series: Block, Bridge, Build: Stories of Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers
episodes.summary: Ariel Fristoe, founder of Out of Hand Theater in Atlanta, describes theater as a civic commons: art to open hearts, information to open minds, conversation to inspire action. She tells how the Decatur Dinners gathered 1,200 strangers in homes for a play and conversation about race, and lays out her vision for a new federal theater project.
ideas: Theater began as a civic commons and can be one again
Every program should leave people hopeful, connected and ready to act
A new federal theatre project could put artists to work on community challenges
approaches: Artists in public service (CETA and its successors)

episodes.title: Paola Mendoza - What if the Most Powerful Antidote for Tyranny is an Artist with a Story?
series: Block, Bridge, Build: Stories of Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers
episodes.summary: Filmmaker, novelist and organizer Paola Mendoza, daughter of Colombian immigrants, talks about two decades of telling immigrant stories through film, theater, public art and literature. She discusses art's role in resisting authoritarianism, her novel Sanctuary, and artists' No ICE in the Cup campaign around the 2026 World Cup.
ideas: Stories expand who counts and who belongs
Art is a force against tyranny
Communities of care in dangerous times

episodes.title: Arts Freedom Weather Report - Who Speaks - Who Belongs?
episodes.summary: An Arts Freedom Weather Report tying together turmoil at the Kennedy Center, America250, the World Cup, Pride festivals and immigrant-rights organizing around one question: who belongs in America's story? Bill describes artists moving from expression to civic practice.
ideas: Belonging may be the central cultural and political battleground
Creative action is evolving from expression to civic practice
Conflicts over institutions are conflicts over who writes the national story

episodes.title: Cynthia Cohen - Acting together on the World Stage
episodes.summary: Peacebuilding scholar Cynthia Cohen reflects on a lifetime of work on arts, culture and conflict transformation, from Jewish-Palestinian dialogue projects in Boston to initiatives in Peru, Sri Lanka, Serbia and Northern Ireland. Voices from her Acting Together project, including John O'Neal and Dijana Milošević, describe theater made to survive tyranny.
ideas: Listening may be the most important creative and civic skill
Artists create spaces where competing truths can be held
Creativity and conflict transformation strengthen democracy under pressure

episodes.title: Veteran Sean Martin Talks About War, Music, PTSD, & Social Change
series: Block, Bridge, Build: Stories of Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers
episodes.summary: Musician, songwriter and Iraq War veteran Sean Martin describes how songwriting, cognitive behavioral therapy and exposure therapy helped him live with PTSD and reclaim agency. Through his songs 'Skeleton Chair' and 'Unspoken' with his band the Quarantined, he talks about war, truth-telling, James Baldwin and artists' responsibility to speak hard truths.
ideas: Disciplined creative practice can help heal what doctors miss
Confronting 'the unspoken' is at the heart of healing and of art
Art can be a vehicle for critical thinking
approaches: Arts in health and arts on prescription

episodes.title: Why Lasting Cultural Partnerships Drive Art & Social Change Success!
episodes.summary: Bill returns to a lesson from the California prison system in 1983: incarcerated artist Verne McKee's ten rules for trust and collaboration, the basis of 'Verne's Rules.' He uses them to explain what separates real cross-sector partnership from outreach, and what artists and institutions owe the communities they invite in.
ideas: Trust, not funding or good intentions, is the currency of partnership
Verne's ten rules show what helps collaborations thrive and what predicts failure
Communities deserve more than one-time projects

episodes.title: Derek Goldman: What Happens When the Stranger Walks In Your Shoes?
series: Block, Bridge, Build: Stories of Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers
episodes.summary: Theater artist and educator Derek Goldman shares his In Your Shoes process, in which two people talk deeply, transcribe the conversation and perform each other's words. He describes using it with conservative Christian and progressive students, in prisons, hospitals and conflict zones, and through Georgetown's Laboratory for Global Performance and Politics.
ideas: In Your Shoes turns strangers into collaborators through radical listening
Democracy needs the freedom to speak vulnerably and be heard
Artists can work across sectors to rebuild trust and civic imagination
orgs: Laboratory for Global Performance and Politics
Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health

episodes.title: Organization & Imagination - What Happens When Actvist Artists Take Root in the System
episodes.summary: Bill tells the story of Barbara Steveni and the Artist Placement Group, British artists who from the late 1960s placed artists inside corporations, railways, steel mills and government ministries, not to decorate those systems but to complicate them. The episode asks why artists may do their best work deep inside the institutions shaping public life.
ideas: Artists may work best inside the systems shaping public life, not at the edges
Attention and metaphor can make institutions more self-aware
Imagination inside organizations is disruptive and necessary

episodes.title: Are Art & Upheaval Incompatible or Inevitable? You Decide
episodes.summary: A 2022 episode rebroadcast with a new introduction. Built around Bill's song and book Art and Upheaval, it revisits artists working in places of conflict, including South Africa, Cambodia after the Khmer Rouge, the Watts Writers Workshop after the 1965 uprising, and DAH Teatar under Milošević in Serbia.
ideas: Art is operational, not ornamental, in times of crisis
After rupture, creative acts stitch communities back together
Imagination is a tool for reshaping reality
orgs: Reyum Institute of Arts and Culture

episodes.title: Suzanne Firstenberg Asks: How Can Art Help Make the Unseen Visible When People Look Away?
series: Block, Bridge, Build: Stories of Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers
episodes.summary: Social practice artist Suzanne Firstenberg talks about In America: Remember, a field of more than 600,000 white flags on the National Mall honoring Americans who died of COVID-19, and her installations on addiction and trauma. She argues that anger is often grief in disguise and asks whether we can 'be we again.'
ideas: Art can make the unseen visible when people look away
Anger is often grief in disguise
Community is the mechanism of healing

episodes.title: Anne Cleveland - How Arts-infused Education Supports Democracy
episodes.summary: Waldorf educator Anne Cleveland, Bill's sister, explains how arts-infused education builds the capacities democracy needs. Children practice attention, empathy, self-regulation and collaboration every day through music, movement, storytelling and class plays, with rhythm and ritual helping them feel grounded and connected.
ideas: Children practice democratic life daily through shared creative work
Arts integration builds attention, empathy and self-regulation
Rhythm and repetition ground children in their bodies and in community
orgs: Association of Waldorf Schools of North America

episodes.title: ART IS CHANGE – ART IS RESISTANCE
episodes.summary: A solo episode on how artists have resisted narrowing freedom of expression. Bill tells four stories: Mexican muralists after the revolution, Billie Holiday's 'Strange Fruit' at Café Society in 1939, Augusto Boal's Theatre of the Oppressed under Brazil's military rule, and Pussy Riot's 2012 protest in Moscow.
ideas: Resistance is cultural, emotional and imaginative, not only political
Art can make an ignored truth impossible to unhear
Rehearsing freedom on stage makes it harder to take away

episodes.title: Jordan Seaberry - What Use is Art Making When Freedom is Under Fire?
episodes.summary: Painter, organizer and educator Jordan Seaberry traces his path from Chicago's South Side to the Rhode Island School of Design, prisoners' rights organizing, Roger Williams University School of Law and leadership of the U.S. Department of Arts and Culture. He argues that listening sits at the heart of both art and organizing, and that artists build real civic power by joining movements.
ideas: Creativity is not extra; it is a civic practice
Listening is central to both art and organizing
Artists build power by joining movements and building alternative systems
orgs: US Department of Arts and Culture
Roger Williams University School of Law

episodes.title: Artist Proof Studio - What Can We Learn From Activist Artists in South Africa
series: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists In...
episodes.summary: Bill retells a story from Art and Upheaval about Artist Proof Studio, a Johannesburg printmaking studio founded in 1991 by Kim Berman. Artists divided by apartheid learned to work together, survived a fire and a death, and built a lasting practice, alongside the story of South Africa's Constitutional Court built as a work of art on the site of a prison.
ideas: Creativity can become infrastructure for a new democracy
A collective studio where artists divided by apartheid learn to work together
Culture does long work that politics alone can't finish

episodes.title: Is Community Based-art Making at the Heart of Cultural Democracy?
episodes.summary: Community arts organizer and theater maker Mat Schwarzman describes his mission to make collaborative art-making a normal part of everyday life. He traces his path from CETA-era arts jobs in Philadelphia to organizing in Oakland and youth theater in post-Katrina New Orleans, and the influence of John O'Neal's story circle method.
ideas: Community arts is a learnable, cross-sector civic practice
Youth arts can be a modern rite of passage into civic voice
Storytelling and collective creation sustain democratic life
approaches: Artists in public service (CETA and its successors)

episodes.title: Joni Doherty: ART IN ACTION Is Fueling Free Expression & Democracy
episodes.summary: Opening the Art in Action series, Joni Doherty of the Kettering Foundation describes how a rediscovered 1964 Martin Luther King Jr. speech in Dayton sparked Visual Voices, a multidisciplinary project of artists, poets and dancers. She explains how the foundation's co-creative approach supports artists confronting censorship and recovering buried histories.
ideas: A forgotten MLK speech sparked a multidisciplinary arts movement in Dayton
Artists confront censorship by reclaiming hidden histories
Creativity may be democracy's most powerful engine

episodes.title: Arts Freedom Weather Report - The MAGA Squeeze Is Provoking Creative Resistance
episodes.summary: An Arts Freedom Weather Report on 'the MAGA squeeze': federal reviews and executive orders reshaping museums, park signage and historical interpretation. Bill tracks the response, from citizen historians documenting Smithsonian changes to artists leaving the Kennedy Center and librarians and educators defending access to history.
ideas: Citizen historians are documenting changes to museum exhibits before they disappear
Artists are walking away from institutions where politics threatens integrity
Cultural workers are building parallel civic infrastructure

episodes.title: Arts ON Prescription: Radical Art & Social Change in Healthcare
episodes.summary: A rebroadcast of the conversation with researchers Jill Sonke and Tasha Golden about 'Arts on Prescription: A Field Guide for US Communities,' which explains how health providers can refer patients to arts, culture and nature, drawing on Massachusetts' CultureRX pilots and research worldwide.
ideas: Health is generated in communities, not only in clinics
Arts on prescription looks different in every community
Research links arts participation to mental health and lower care costs
approaches: Arts in health and arts on prescription
orgs: University of Florida Center for Arts in Medicine
International Arts + Mind Lab at Johns Hopkins Medicine

episodes.title: The Wedding - What Can We Learn From Activist Artists in Northern Ireland?
series: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists In...
episodes.summary: Bill revisits The Wedding, a 1999 Belfast community play devised by Protestants and Catholics after the Good Friday Agreement and performed in kitchen houses on both sides of a peace line. He draws three lessons for a divided United States: proximity changes people, shared labor builds trust before shared opinion, and hope is a container built through practice.
ideas: Proximity and intimacy make caricature impossible
Shared labor builds trust before shared opinion
Hope is not a feeling but a container built through practice

episodes.title: The Intercessor - Art, Faith, & Repair in the MAGA Maelstrom
episodes.summary: Writer and cultural activist Arlene Goldbard talks about her novel The Intercessor, which explores how people in unstable times can stay in relationship and ethical choice instead of surrendering to charismatic leaders or false certainty. They discuss intercession as discernment, artists as bridges, and repair as a practiced skill.
ideas: Intercession as a practice of discernment and listening
Artists can help communities resist the pull toward false certainty
Repair is a practiced skill that needs mutual accountability

episodes.title: Meeting The Moment -  Tactics & Tools for Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers
episodes.summary: An Arts Freedom Weather Report on the tools and tactics artists are using against authoritarian pressure, from the Minneapolis singing marches to banned-book actions, artist-led billboards and censorship flashpoints. Bill points to networks such as Beautiful Trouble and the Center for Artistic Activism that teach resistance as a craft.
ideas: Artists are turning public space into sites of creative resistance
Local, place-based responses are laboratories for cultural democracy
Artist networks are teaching resistance as a craft

episodes.title: Arts Freedom Weather Report: MINNEAPOLIS JAN. 2026
episodes.summary: An Arts Freedom Weather Report from Minneapolis in January 2026, after two killings and a surge of federal immigration enforcement. David O'Fallon describes singing vigils, decentralized mutual aid and rapid-response arts support, and poet Marquis Bowie reflects on grief, policing and the writing healing circle he leads.
ideas: Culture moves faster than institutions in a crisis
Resistance can be hundreds of small, locally rooted acts with no single leader
Imagination is a survival skill when fear is used to limit it

episodes.title: Alan Jenkins: These Art & Social Change Superpowers Can Help Save Democracy
episodes.summary: Civil rights lawyer, former Ford Foundation human rights director and Harvard Law professor Alan Jenkins, co-author of 1/6: The Graphic Novel, talks about story as power. He traces how law, policy and culture shape public belief, how popular culture from Superman to Persepolis has confronted authoritarianism, and what hybrid leadership looks like.
ideas: Story is inseparable from power
Popular culture has long been used to confront authoritarianism
Empathy and imagination matter as much as expertise in hybrid leadership
orgs: NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund

episodes.title: The Arts Freedom Weather Report - January 2026
episodes.summary: The January 2026 Arts Freedom Weather Report sets a cultural baseline for the year: how culture is being targeted through funding shifts, legal pressure and narrative control at the NEA, public media, museums and universities, and how artists are responding. Musicians and companies withdrawing from the Kennedy Center are among the examples.
ideas: Culture is being strategically targeted through funding, law and narrative control
Small policy shifts stack up as institutions recalibrate
Resistance is a learned practice, like disciplined improvisation

episodes.title: METRA - A Climate Revolution With Songs
episodes.summary: Theater director Emily Hartford and composer Ned Hartford discuss Metra: A Climate Revolution with Songs, a nine-episode musical audio drama that reimagines a Greek myth as a near-future climate story. They talk about music reaching places facts can't, telling climate stories without fear-mongering, and building art others can use.
ideas: Music and the human voice reach where facts and lectures can't
A climate story can be told without 'disaster porn'
Art can be cultural infrastructure, not a one-off production

episodes.title: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists in Australia: PART 2
series: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists In...
episodes.summary: Part two of the BIGhART story follows Scott Rankin and Australia's leading arts and social change organization into skate culture in Tasmania, using skateboarding, Indigenous wisdom and long-term creative process to support marginalized young people and defend the Tarkine rainforest.
ideas: Skateboarding can be both an art form and a mental health lifeline
Projects that unfold over decades challenge quick-fix activism
Creativity rooted in respect, reciprocity and humility

episodes.title: Goodbye Leni Sloan: Artist, Activist, Catalyst
episodes.summary: A special remembrance of Leni (Lenwood O.) Sloan: artist, activist and Bill's close friend. Bill traces Leni's life from his Bicentennial musical The Wake about Black minstrelsy to decades of work uncovering erased Black histories and shaking institutions awake.
ideas: History lives in bodies and culture breathes through people
The real work is connection between past and present
Telling the whole truth, especially the hard parts, keeps us human

episodes.title: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists in Australia? Part 1
series: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists In...
episodes.summary: Part one of the BIGhART story: Scott Rankin describes Australia's Big hART and its projects Ngapartji Ngapartji and the Namatjira Project, which used performance and community-led storytelling to support Indigenous language, land and cultural rights and to reclaim stolen intellectual property.
ideas: 'It's harder to hurt someone if you know their story'
Community-led creativity can dismantle colonial narratives
Visibility for unheard voices requires virtuosity

episodes.title: Why Should Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers Care About Sustainability?
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: In the sixth Building Blocks episode, Bill, Leni Sloan and Barbara Schaffer Bacon ask why sustainability matters when residencies are short and funding cycles brief. They treat sustainability as an ethical responsibility carried by relationships, trust and the passing of creative values across generations, not as institutional survival.
ideas: Sustainability is an ethical responsibility, not longevity for its own sake
Relationships can outlast grants and funding cycles
Some forms of change are too important to be temporary

episodes.title: Why Are Humility & Failure Essential to Art and Social Change Success?
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: The fifth Building Blocks episode: Leni Sloan, Barbara Schaffer Bacon and Bill trade stories on how humility and failure shape community arts work, from Leni taking a 12-line role in Richard II to a Sacramento public art controversy and a San Quentin poet who left a Broadway star speechless.
ideas: Stay porous and humble enough to learn what the work is teaching
Failure can crack a project open so a truer version can emerge
No one is ever done learning, not even the masters

episodes.title: What are the Moral & Ethical Challenges Facing Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers?
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: The fourth Building Blocks episode asks what artists owe the communities they hope to serve when good intentions aren't enough. Bill, Leni Sloan and Barbara Schaffer Bacon discuss the ethical weight of working in places marked by trauma and power imbalance, including a prison songwriting class where one creative moment had life-or-death stakes.
ideas: Good intentions aren't enough
Artists must weigh the ethics of their presence in places of trauma
Art trivialized by society is still potent enough to heal or harm

episodes.title: How Robert Farid Karimi Uses COMEDY & FOOD as a Powerful Strategy for Social Change
episodes.summary: A rebroadcast conversation with comedian, chef, poet and educator Robert Farid Karimi, also known as the People's Chef. He explains how humor and shared cooking can bridge conflict-ridden communities, the power of gossip in immigrant cultures, and what organizers can learn from Mel Brooks and Cheech and Chong.
ideas: Humor can lift a room and bridge a divided community
The fool and gossip have power in a post-truth era
Play helps people see themselves as storytellers

episodes.title: Art, Agency, & Fear: How Artmaking Can Help Crush the MAGA Monsters at the Door
episodes.summary: A short solo episode on fear and agency. Bill explains how fear hijacks the brain's reasoning center and argues that making things, from pots to poems, can restore a sense of agency and connection, making creativity an ancient antidote to what he calls the MAGA fear machine.
ideas: Fear and agency are twin engines, and imagination decides which gets fuel
Making things can rewire the brain and restore hope
Shared creativity is an ancient antidote to manufactured fear

episodes.title: Should Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers be Running for Office - Tom Tresser Says, "ABSOLUTELY!"
episodes.summary: Chicago civic organizer and self-described 'public defender' Tom Tresser argues that artists and the nonprofit sector are missing in action on power and policy, and should run for office. He tells how a small, unfunded coalition stopped the 2016 Olympics from coming to Chicago and why artistic and political skills are cut from the same cloth.
ideas: Creatives should stop 'staying in their lane' and lead in civic life
A small unfunded coalition can beat powerful interests
Artistic skills and political strategy are cut from the same cloth
approaches: Artists in politics and running for office

episodes.title: What Can We Learn from Activist Artists in Singapore?
series: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists In...
episodes.summary: A rebroadcast of the 2021 conversation with Su-Lin Ngiam, co-founder of ArtsWok Collaborative in Singapore, with a new introduction comparing 'flawed democracies.' She describes using inflatable theaters and site-specific installations to hold space for taboo subjects like death and inequality in a tightly regulated city-state.
ideas: Artists as 'agents of hope' bridging differences
Public art makes the invisible visible and the unheard heard
The artist as intermediary across sectors and beliefs

episodes.title: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists In Serbia?
series: What Can We Learn From Activist Artists In...
episodes.summary: Revisits the 2022 conversation with Dijana Milošević of Belgrade's DAH Teatar and catches up on the company. The episode recounts the 1992 street performance This Babylonian Confusion staged during war, and newer projects: Invisible City, performed on city buses, and Dancing Trees, in which a forest becomes collaborator.
ideas: 'We can oppose destruction and violence with the creation of meaning'
A theater company restructured to sustain creative risk
Performance on buses and among trees reaches beyond theatergoers

episodes.title: Five Arts Superpowers for Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers to Make Change NOW!
episodes.summary: A solo episode asking what use art is in unsettling times. Bill invites listeners to sing Ella's Song, then draws on Ella Baker, Bernice Johnson Reagon and the 1957 San Quentin production of Waiting for Godot to name what art does in chaos: help us notice, connect and rebuild trust.
ideas: Art helps us pay attention to our world, neighbors and selves
Making together builds creative trust
Story and performance can bridge divides, even behind bars

episodes.title: Emma Addams: Can a Quilt Change how Congress Listens— & How you Practice Democracy at Home?
episodes.summary: Emma Petty Addams, co-executive director of Mormon Women for Ethical Government, tells how Quilting for the Constitution grew from a 48-hour idea in Provo, Utah to 62 quilts delivered to 56 congressional offices, involving more than 5,000 people. She describes peacemaking as daily, local practice in PTOs, churches and quilt-ins.
ideas: Treat conflict as raw material and democracy as daily local practice
Artful collaboration turns advocacy into community building
Build trust and persuasion where you live, not through outrage

episodes.title: How is the Government Threatening Activist Artists and Arts Organization?
episodes.summary: A weather report on threats to activist artists and arts organizations from the federal government: NEA grant restrictions struck down in court, loyalty-style clauses in state sub-grants, Florida's veto of all state arts funding and cuts at the NEH. Bill outlines what may be coming and the legal and advocacy resources defending the field.
ideas: Funding is being pulled and loyalty-style clauses added to grants
Nonprofit and tax-exempt status may become pressure points
Get expert counsel and don't go it alone
orgs: Institute of Museum and Library Services

episodes.title: Liz Sunde Brings Music To Life: Activist Artists Making Music, Making Change, & Thriving
episodes.summary: Liz Sunde, founder of Music to Life, describes how a songwriting contest grew into a six-and-a-half-month accelerator that helps musicians design, fund and measure community projects while making a living. Examples include Vanessa Lively's Home Street Music with unhoused neighbors in Austin and Myles Bullen's poet-healer work inside prisons.
ideas: Artists can make change while making a living
Musicians can move from stage talent to creative problem-solvers
Training, coaching and seed grants help artists build sustainable projects

episodes.title: Solar Story Circle: How Narrative Powers Democracy & Social Change
episodes.summary: Drawing on Bill McKibben's book Here Comes the Sun, Bill compares the spread of cheap solar power, built by farmers in places like Pakistan, to the power of shared stories. He argues that story circles, neighbors telling each other what they see and feel, can work like a solar array for democracy against narratives of fear and scarcity.
ideas: Hope backed by data: solar is spreading from the ground up
Stories of fear and scarcity can be replaced with stories of abundance
Story circles can power democracy the way panels power homes

episodes.title: Alma & Frank: Designing Creative Futures One Story at a Time
episodes.summary: Part two with Alma Robinson of California Lawyers for the Arts introduces Designing Creative Futures, which has placed more than 200 formerly incarcerated people in paid internships with arts organizations. Participant Frank Quiroz tells how mentorship and woodworking in prison, then an internship, helped him build a new life.
ideas: Creative work can be a literal job offer after prison
Mentorship and belief in potential lead to lasting change
Craft and persistence reshape reentry with dignity
orgs: Los Angeles County Museum of Art

episodes.title: Alma Robinson: How Do You Build an Art & Social Change Movement That Lasts Decades
episodes.summary: Alma Robinson, longtime executive director of California Lawyers for the Arts, traces her path from research on African art restitution to leading the coalition that revived arts programs in California prisons, which grew to $8 million a year by 2016. She also discusses threats to nonprofits and DEI work, and why she remains optimistic.
ideas: Systemic change rests on collaboration and cross-sector alliances
Art is a lifeline, from youth engagement to prison rehabilitation
Evidence and data win over legislators where stories alone don't
orgs: California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation

episodes.title: Art and Resistance: Smithsonian, FREE DC, LA, and Beyond
episodes.summary: A weather report on the administration's attacks on the Smithsonian under Executive Order 14253 and the responses: Free DC's go-go block parties reclaiming public space, Los Angeles cultural organizations speaking out during ICE raids, and Detroit Opera's production of The Central Park Five.
ideas: Executive Order 14253 is reshaping cultural institutions
Music-fueled protest can reclaim public space
Cultural organizers are coordinating statements of defiance
orgs: National Museum of African American History and Culture
LA Plaza de Cultura y Artes

episodes.title: The Community Bridge: How can activist artists help build the bridges we need to make democracy whole?
episodes.summary: Bill tells the story of the Community Bridge, a five-year mural project that turned a plain concrete bridge in Frederick, Maryland into a trompe l'oeil work built from thousands of residents' ideas across race, age and geography. When a forgotten maintenance commitment let the mural decay, the community's response became an act of healing and recovery.
ideas: One bold question sparked a flood of community voices
A painted illusion became a real bridge between people
Shared creations need care, and restoring them can heal
approaches: Artists in public service (CETA and its successors)

episodes.title: Wendy Shenefelt: How Can Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers Become a Real Force For Resistance & Change?
episodes.summary: Wendy Shenefelt, who grew up in the Deep South in a transracial family, describes her path to becoming a convener and leader in Alternate ROOTS, a 49-year-old network of Southern artists and cultural workers. She talks about art cutting through when words aren't enough, keeping a community safe and connected, and the value of quiet work behind the scenes.
ideas: Art can cut through the noise when words aren't enough
Communities must hold both joy and grief to stay resilient
Sometimes the smartest move is to work quietly behind the scenes

episodes.title: Self-Care: Why it Matters for Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers!
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: The third Building Blocks episode: Bill, Leni Sloan and Barbara Schaffer Bacon talk about self-care for cultural workers as a structural necessity, from housing, health care and childcare to burnout, soul-feeding practices and ecosystems of mutual care.
ideas: Self-care is a structural necessity, not a bubble bath
Untangling identity from work is part of sustaining it
Community care starts with care for the people doing the work

episodes.title: Can Artist activists and cultural organizers become trusted community leaders?
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: The second Building Blocks episode asks whether artists can become trusted community leaders. Bill, Leni Sloan and Barbara Schaffer Bacon reframe leadership through the wedding planner, the parade leader and the 'prickly cactus,' with stories from death row, neighborhood schools and an internment camp.
ideas: Many cultural activists are already community leaders
Leadership metaphors: wedding planner, parade leader, soul shepherd
Lead with courage, communication and care in complex settings
orgs: Social and Public Art Resource Center (SPARC)

episodes.title: What Are Activist Artists & Cultural Organizers Accountable to in Their Work?
series: Building Blocks of Effective Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: The first Building Blocks episode asks to whom and to what activist artists are accountable. Bill, Barbara Schaffer Bacon and Leni Sloan discuss cultural competency, trust-building and the layered responsibilities artists carry, with examples like Marty Pottenger's police poetry project in Portland, Maine.
ideas: Deep cultural competency and trust are essential to community-based art
Artists carry layered responsibilities to craft and community
Accountability can inspire civic connection

episodes.title: Jerry Stropnicky: Story, Civic Empathy, & Social Change
episodes.summary: Stage director and playwright Jerry Stropnicky describes going only where he is invited to make ensemble-based community theater, with projects that have addressed the opioid epidemic and flood recovery and even reshaped local policy. He shares his 'Seven A's,' principles for ethical, effective community arts practice from agency to accessibility.
ideas: Go only where you're invited; never parachute in
Community story-making builds civic empathy and can reshape policy
Seven principles guide ethical community arts, from agency to accessibility

episodes.title: “How Do Activist Artists and Cultural Organizers Resist: Lessons from the Anti-Authoritarian Frontlines
episodes.summary: Bill reports from the 22nd Century Initiative gathering in Atlanta, where movement leaders asked how to stop the rise of authoritarianism. Drawing on Daniel Hunter, Maria Stephan and Ash-Lee Woodard Henderson, he covers proven nonviolent resistance strategies, loneliness as fuel for authoritarianism, and artists as strategic players in defending democracy.
ideas: Nonviolent resistance has toppled regimes and strengthened democracies
Loneliness fuels authoritarianism; art can reconnect communities
Artists are strategic players, not just inspiration

episodes.title: Can Arts Festivals, Community Theater & Cultural Organizers Save Democracy?
episodes.summary: Theater maker and former mayor Kathie deNobriga of Pine Lake, Georgia talks about moving from political theater to small-town leadership, and what 50 years with Alternate ROOTS taught her about building the beloved community through festivals, community theater, story circles, humor and humility.
ideas: Listening, laughter and shared purpose build community
Festivals and community theater can be secret weapons for tolerance
Humility and mistakes are essential to resilient communities
approaches: Artists in politics and running for office

episodes.title: When the Arts Are Under Fire – Navigating Today’s Unfriendly Cultural Climate
episodes.summary: A weather report on the rising political and legal pressure on arts nonprofits doing equity work, from revoked NEA grants to cuts to public media. Drawing on a Grantmakers in the Arts webinar, Bill contrasts 'Ironman' and 'Atomic Blonde' survival strategies and shares tools for crisis communication, narrative layering and coalition building.
ideas: Federal policy shifts are undermining equity-focused arts work
Different survival strategies fit different missions
Crisis communication and coalitions protect organizations under pressure

episodes.title: Can Activist Artists Bring DEI Back From the Dead? Part 3
series: Bring DEI Back from the Dead
episodes.summary: The last of the three-part Breaking Ice series moves from stage to synapse. Bill shares a layperson's tour of the neuroscience of imagination, fear, empathy and storytelling, and why performance is a powerful tool for changing how we see 'the other.'
ideas: Neuroscience can help explain the human struggle with difference
Performance can reconfigure how we perceive 'the other'
Shared experience can rewire hearts and minds

episodes.title: Can Theater Artists Bring DEI Back From the Dead? Part 2
series: Bring DEI Back from the Dead
episodes.summary: Chapter two of the Breaking Ice series follows the 2019 Barnes Jewish Hospital performance into its final scenes and the post-performance debrief, where hospital staff and actors work through fear, defensiveness and responsibility. Cast and audience members reflect on how improvisation, humor and empathy opened them to change.
ideas: The real work begins when the performance ends
Improvisation, humor and empathy defuse defensiveness
Naming what you're afraid of opens honest conversation

episodes.title: Can Activist Theater Artists Bring DEI Back from the Dead? Part 1
series: Bring DEI Back from the Dead
episodes.summary: First of a three-part series pushing back against the dismantling of DEI. Bill takes listeners inside a Breaking Ice performance at Barnes Jewish Hospital in St. Louis, where Pillsbury House + Theatre actors stage workplace scenes of bias, privilege and immigration fears for about 200 hospital staff, and company members trace the program's history back to Living Stage.
ideas: DEI values are rooted in America's founding struggle to live up to its ideals
Unresolved scenes show bias as an ongoing condition, not a problem to be solved once
Theater holds a mirror to a workplace's own culture so staff recognize themselves
orgs: People's Institute for Survival and Beyond

episodes.title: Art IS Change: Want Proof That Art Makes Real Change? Start Here
episodes.summary: Marking the podcast's name change from Change the Story / Change the World to Art Is Change, Bill debates his inner skeptic 'Billy Rio' about why the change matters. He argues that artists are central to rewriting damaging narratives, citing Lily Yeh's Village of Arts and Humanities in Philadelphia and clown-led protests in Serbia.
ideas: The new name aims to make activist artists more visible and impactful
Artists counter dominant, damaging narratives
Real stories show art reshaping communities

episodes.title: Julia Roig Believes Arts Activism & Cultural Organizing are a Pro Democracy Imperative
episodes.summary: Peacebuilder and organizer Julia Roig describes the Horizons Project, spun off in 2021 to weave relationships across movements for democracy and justice. She explains why storytelling, play, vulnerability and cultural engagement are essential strategies for countering authoritarianism and why current systems often fail to support artist-activist collaboration.
ideas: Arts and culture can be the connective tissue of social movements
Relationship weaving is a form of movement-building
Play and vulnerability are essential strategies, not extras

episodes.title: The CETA Arts Revolution Part 2: What Can Today's Activist Artists Learn From It?
episodes.summary: Part two with artists and historians Virginia Maksymowicz and Blaise Tobia on the 1970s CETA arts program's legacy. They describe how it informs pandemic-era programs like Creatives Rebuild New York, and share stories of the negotiation, humility and adaptability artists need in community work but never learn in art school.
ideas: CETA's community-centered model inspires today's artist employment programs
Artists need skills like negotiation and humility that art school doesn't teach
Art can be community infrastructure
approaches: Artists in public service (CETA and its successors)
orgs: New York Foundation for the Arts

episodes.title: THE CETA ARTS REVOLUTION: What Can Today's Activist Artists & Organizers Learn from It?
episodes.summary: Artists turned historians Virginia Maksymowicz and Blaise Tobia uncover the forgotten story of the 1970s CETA arts program, which employed more than 20,000 artists and creative staff, the largest U.S. investment in art and culture. They describe how it embedded artists in communities and planted organizations like BACA Downtown and Philadelphia's Painted Bride.
ideas: A forgotten federal jobs program was the largest U.S. investment in the arts
CETA embedded artists in the heart of local communities
Its history offers a blueprint for art as public service
approaches: Artists in public service (CETA and its successors)

episodes.title: New Rules: 11 Unlikely Lessons for Activist Artists Navigating MAGA.
episodes.summary: Drawing on his years running California's Arts in Corrections program in the 1980s and work in Cambodia, Serbia and Northern Ireland, Bill offers 11 rules for activist artists navigating today's authoritarian climate, from building credibility in divided settings to avoiding us-versus-them traps and protecting mental health.
ideas: Credibility and respect are earned in high-stakes, divided settings
Long-term commitment beats one-time activism
Tell bold but responsible stories and protect your own wellbeing
orgs: Vacaville Prison Art and Musicians Guilds

episodes.title: How are Artists and Organizers Creating a Better World Together? Reprise
episodes.summary: A reprise of the 2024 conversation with labor strategist Ken Grossinger about his book Art Works. He explains why organizers can't work effectively without culture and how art drives the narrative shifts that movements depend on, with examples from a Louisville museum exhibit to musicians defending Alaska's Bristol Bay.
ideas: Organizers can't work effectively without culture
Policy changes fade, but stories have staying power
Artists and organizers need to think strategically together

episodes.title: Change the Story Weather Report: A Neighborhood Cultural Center Navigates the MAGA Storm
episodes.summary: A weather report from Minneapolis's Powderhorn neighborhood with Noel Raymond of Pillsbury House + Theatre, a few blocks from George Floyd Square. She describes the fear, rage and disorientation artists and neighbors feel, and how sanctuary, joy, story circles and cultural expression become forms of defiance.
ideas: Disorientation is a tactic to prevent resistance; naming it helps
Sanctuary is both safety and strategy
Spaces of joy and community stories are a lifeline

episodes.title: Talking Walls & Dancing Kites*: Powerful Lessons from a Prison Writing Classroom
episodes.summary: Poet and professor Jim Reese talks about more than a decade as writer in residence at the federal prison camp in Yankton, South Dakota, through an NEA program. He describes incarcerated men finding their voices and reconnecting with family through writing, and how the work reshaped his own ideas of justice, redemption and the artist's role.
ideas: Writing helps incarcerated people find their voices and reconnect with family
Teaching in prison reshapes ideas of justice and redemption
Authentic connection breaks barriers in rigid environments

episodes.title: Change the Story Good Trouble Weather Report: Massachusetts
episodes.summary: Michael Bobbitt, executive director of the Mass Cultural Council and Massachusetts' top arts official, discusses the climate for the arts under the Trump administration. He explains why DEI remains central to the agency even if that means rejecting NEA funds, and urges the arts sector to organize its advocacy: 'If you're not at the table, you're on the menu.'
ideas: DEI is central to the mission, even at the cost of federal funds
The arts sector must organize its advocacy like other lobbies
'If you're not at the table, you're on the menu'
approaches: Arts in health and arts on prescription
orgs: Institute of Museum and Library Services

episodes.title: How do Arts Leaders Become Community Change Agents?
episodes.summary: Mass Cultural Council executive director Michael Bobbitt shares how art saved him as a child ('little Michael Bobbitt') and why creative work is inherently political. He calls for Black joy alongside narratives of trauma, critiques the nonprofit arts model, and describes arts prescriptions and sensory-friendly theater.
ideas: Art can be a survival strategy and a lifesaver
Balance narratives of trauma with joy
Arts organizations must think boldly and cross-sectorally
approaches: Arts in health and arts on prescription

episodes.title: CSCW's Art & Social Change Weather Report From Minneapolis
episodes.summary: The first Weather Report: David O'Fallon, a cultural leader with roots in Minneapolis's In the Heart of the Beast Theatre and past roles at the Kennedy Center, NEA and Minnesota Humanities Center, describes how artists and organizers are navigating political upheaval, the unresolved tensions of George Floyd Square, and his vision for a People's Celebration of America in 2026.
ideas: Art is both expression and a force for resistance and healing
George Floyd Square remains a place of tension, dialogue and healing
Practical coalition-building over ideological purity
orgs: In the Heart of the Beast Puppet and Mask Theatre

episodes.title: How the Arts Can Thwart the Attention Bandits
episodes.summary: A solo episode on the attention economy. Through the story of Fletcher, a Midwestern electrician lost in a big-box store's marketing, and Chris Hayes's book The Siren's Call, Bill argues that attention has become a commodity like labor once did, and that consciously using our imaginations is a way to reclaim autonomy.
ideas: Attention is being bought and sold without our permission
Captured attention shapes what people believe and do
Using our imaginations is a way to reclaim agency

episodes.title: Henry Frank: Art & the 21st Century Man
episodes.summary: Two earlier conversations with Henry Frank are combined to tell how he went from a 29-to-life sentence at San Quentin to a celebrated artist, teacher and cultural leader through the William James Association's prison arts program. Bill presents his story as a model of a 21st-century man defined by compassion and humility.
ideas: A new kind of manhood rooted in compassion, forbearance and humility
Art and community can transform a life sentence into a calling
Storytelling helps reimagine identity and foster healing

episodes.title: Lynne Elizabeth: Breaking Ground for The New Village
episodes.summary: Lynne Elizabeth, founding director of New Village Press, describes herself as a 'book doula' and explains how mission-centered publishing elevates voices left out of mainstream narratives. She talks about books like Root Shock and the Beginner's Guide to Community-Based Arts as instruments for social change and the community that grows among authors.
ideas: Publishing with purpose can be a revolutionary act
Books are vessels of change, not just products
Authors rooted in their communities shape narratives of resilience

episodes.title: A Conversation With Lily Yeh
episodes.summary: Community arts pioneer Lily Yeh, co-founder of Philadelphia's Village of Arts and Humanities and founder of Barefoot Artists, talks about decades of using art for healing in places from North Philadelphia to Rwanda, Kenya and China. She stresses listening to people affected by trauma, collaborating on the process, and creating a genocide memorial with a Rwandan community.
ideas: Healing and beauty come from listening, not imposing solutions
The process of making together matters as much as the result
Art helps people reclaim their narratives and rebuild trust

episodes.title: Jack Bowers -A Do-gooder Opportunist in the Joint : A Jazz Improvisation in 4 Parts
episodes.summary: Musician and educator Jack Bowers recalls building the Soledad Prison arts program in California's Arts in Corrections network in the 1980s, part of what Bill calls the largest residential arts program in U.S. history. He describes earning respect from incarcerated artists and staff, teaching music and songwriting, and the 'Zen guitarist' who practiced on a cardboard guitar neck.
ideas: Curiosity and opportunism can build something extraordinary
Respect and permission from inmates and staff let the program thrive
Creativity is a lifeline inside prison

episodes.title: Is Democracy a Creative Practice?  2
episodes.summary: The second of two compilation episodes on democracy as a creative practice. Excerpts feature Arnaldo López and Ben Fink on Roadside Theater's plays in Art in a Democracy, labor organizer Ken Grossinger on arts-based organizing, and Scott Rankin of Australia's Big hART on the ethics of culturally based democratic practice.
ideas: Art can help people find common ground across difference
Storytelling reclaims democratic space for marginalized groups
Cultural democracy honors and celebrates difference

episodes.title: Is Democracy a Creative Practice?
episodes.summary: Recorded right after the 2024 election, Bill argues that American democracy is fragile because people have few chances to practice it, and that democracy should be treated as a creative practice. Excerpts from past guests including Leni Sloan, Carlton Turner, Harry Boyte, Pam Korza and Barbara Schaffer Bacon explore story, culture bearers and citizenship schools.
ideas: Democracy is a practice we haven't been practicing
Sharing personal stories is how democracy is practiced
Creative engagement can bridge divides and build civic life

episodes.title: Jeff Mather: Art, Community, & the Materialized Imagination
episodes.summary: Teaching artist Jeff Mather, a self-described 'public art digital storytelling alchemist' in Georgia, shares stories of making big things with lots of people, including an environmental sculpture built with youth in a neglected West Baltimore park. He talks about proxemics, entering communities with humility, and his work with Alternate ROOTS.
ideas: Involving students builds creativity, agency and responsibility
Reclaimed public spaces open dialogue about safety and ownership
Enter communities with humility and a willingness to learn

episodes.title: Rebecca Rice: Giving Voice to the Invisible
episodes.summary: A theatrical reading of Bill's 1988 conversation with actress, director, teacher and anti-racism activist Rebecca Rice, one of his community arts mentors, with Kathi Bentley voicing Rice. Rice describes growing up in a Chicago community arts program, working with Living Stage, and giving voice to 'invisible' people: prisoners, youth, disabled people and survivors of abuse.
ideas: Every life affects the whole fabric of human existence
Collaborators are partners, not subjects
Community arts carries moral and ethical dimensions beyond technique

episodes.title: Billy Yalowitz: Art & Trust in Treacherous Times
episodes.summary: Theater director and choreographer Billy Yalowitz talks about equitable partnerships between universities and communities, drawing on his years at Temple University and the Black Bottom Performance Project, which gathered stories of a Philadelphia neighborhood razed by urban renewal. He also describes reconnecting with his cultural roots and Indigenous partners in the Hudson Valley around climate justice.
ideas: Know your own heritage before engaging others' stories
University-community collaborations must be equitable and accountable
Collective memory and storytelling can address historical injustice

episodes.title: Laurie Meadoff: What Happens When Art & Humanity Pull Up A Chair?
episodes.summary: Laurie Meadoff, founder of the CityKids Foundation and an Emmy-nominated producer, talks about four decades of arts-based youth development and media work, from CityKids in New York to Chat the Planet, Take Back the Mic: Africa and health and anti-hate initiatives. She stresses listening, community empowerment and turning 'no' into the start of the next story.
ideas: Listening and adaptability drive community empowerment
Young people's creativity can be channeled into activism
Media can connect youth across the world

episodes.title: From Ignorance to Knowing: A Journey of Art, Science & Healing
episodes.summary: Bill tells the story of Dr. Subhasis Banerji, a Singapore bioengineer who recovered from a severe brain and leg injury through yoga and martial arts, then invented SynPhNe, a wearable device that trains brain and body together for stroke rehabilitation. Bill draws parallels to the self-healing he witnessed in prison arts programs.
ideas: Art and science, body and mind, overlap in healing
The human capacity for self-recovery and growth
Creative practice and medical innovation share common ground

episodes.title: BIGhART BIGsTORY REDUX 2
episodes.summary: A rebroadcast of part two of the BIGhART BIGsTORY saga, following Scott Rankin's Big hART into skate culture in Tasmania and its work on Aboriginal land rights, youth mental health and environmental protection across 62 Australian communities.
ideas: Skateboarding as art form and mental health lifeline
Projects that unfold over decades
Creativity rooted in respect, reciprocity and humility

episodes.title: BIGhART BIGsTORY REDUX
episodes.summary: A rebroadcast of part one of the BIGhART BIGsTORY saga. Scott Rankin describes how Big hART grew over 30 years into one of the world's leading arts and social change organizations, including the Ngapartji Ngapartji project with Pitjantjatjara communities, which premiered at the Melbourne International Arts Festival in 2006.
ideas: We imagined our way into this mess and must imagine our way out
It's harder to hurt someone if you know their story
Long-term, community-led projects can change national narratives

episodes.title: Cynthia Cohen: Art, Conflict, Peacebuilding, and Social Change
episodes.summary: Activist, writer, educator and filmmaker Cynthia Cohen discusses her career in arts, culture and conflict transformation, including the Acting Together on the World Stage project with Theatre Without Borders. Voices of creative peacebuilders from Uganda, Argentina, Australia, Palestine and Serbia open the episode, which also pays tribute to Bernice Johnson Reagon.
ideas: Artmaking and peacemaking are mutually supporting community assets
Humility and ethics are core to peacebuilding work
Storytelling and listening drive conflict transformation

episodes.title: Alternate Roots: 50 Years of Artist Activism & Cultural Organizing,
episodes.summary: A bonus episode marking 50 years of Alternate ROOTS, the Southern arts organization dedicated to social and economic justice. ROOTS staffers Aimee McCoy and Clarissa Crawford discuss the role of membership, members as change agents, power and agency within the organization, and the 2024 Roots Week gathering.
ideas: An arts service organization thriving for half a century
Members are the change agents
Roots Week as a gathering of creativity and community

episodes.title: Reports Later: Why We Still Struggle with Race and Belonging—And How Public Art Can Change That – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two of the conversation with Lenwood 'Leni' Sloan covers the co-opting of 'woke,' the meaning of Juneteenth, replacing Confederate monuments, the 14th Amendment, and nine reports on the arts and race. He describes public art and collective storytelling, like the Eighth Ward monument and Waystation projects, as ways to build community dialogue.
ideas: Public art can foster community dialogue and healing
Democracy means citizenship and communal responsibility, not just voting
Relearning to walk as a metaphor for social balance

episodes.title: Reports Later: Why We Still Struggle With Race and Belonging—And How Public Art Can Change That – Part 1
episodes.summary: The 100th episode is a rambling, reflective conversation with longtime friend Lenwood 'Leni' Sloan, activist, actor, dancer, playwright, impresario and historian. They talk about recovery and perseverance, the pandemic's social toll, the untold story of Lydia Hamilton Smith, the culture wars, and a call to action for citizen artists.
ideas: Imagination and decision-making carry us through pain
Untold histories like Lydia Hamilton Smith's deserve to be told
Citizen artists are called to act

episodes.title: Animating Democracy: Can Activist Artists and Cultural Organizing Help Save it  - Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with Barbara Schaffer Bacon and Pam Korza, co-directors of Animating Democracy, explores case studies of arts-based civic dialogue: restoring a King Kamehameha statue in Kohala, Hawaii; Liz Lerman's Shipyard Project in Portsmouth; Sojourn Theatre in Lima, Ohio; and museum exhibits on genomics, the Holocaust and lynching. They also discuss how the field has evolved.
ideas: Arts projects can build trust and open difficult conversations
A framework for assessing civic outcomes of art
The field of arts-based civic engagement has grown and changed

episodes.title: Animating Democracy: Can Activist Artists and Cultural Organizing Help Save it  - Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one with Animating Democracy co-directors Pam Korza and Barbara Schaffer Bacon asks whether the arts can help save American democracy. They trace arts-based civic dialogue through the AIDS Memorial Quilt, The Vagina Monologues, The Laramie Project and Traces of the Trade, and how Animating Democracy supported such work in communities nationwide.
ideas: Democracy is a creative practice of hands as well as heads and hearts
It's harder to hurt someone if you know their story
Engaging divisive issues through art can heal deep social wounds

episodes.title: How Judith Marcuse Transformed a Life in Dance into a Movement for Social Change
episodes.summary: Canadian dancer, choreographer and producer Judith Marcuse traces 40 years of work from 1960s London to youth-centered, issue-based projects like ICE, FIRE and EARTH and the 2006 World Urban Festival. She explains why connecting head, heart and body is central to art for social change, and how she and partners built a new collective creative practice.
ideas: Embodiment connects head, heart and body
Art for social change is made by a collective creative community
Youth-centered, issue-based projects can run for years

episodes.title: How are Artist Activists and Organizers Creating a Better World Together? Reprise
episodes.summary: Labor strategist Ken Grossinger, longtime SEIU and AFL-CIO strategist, explains why organizers can't work effectively without culture and why art drives the narrative shifts movements need. He discusses his book Art Works, from a museum exhibit in Louisville to musicians defending Alaska's Bristol Bay.
ideas: Organizers can't work effectively without culture
Policy changes fade, but stories have staying power
Power analysis plus artistic expression amplifies campaigns

episodes.title: Jose Antonio Aguirre on Cultural Organizing, and the Power of Public Art
episodes.summary: Mexico City-born muralist Jose Antonio Aguirre, known for Venetian glass mosaic and carved limestone murals, describes four decades of public art between two cultures. He recounts his path from a Chicago trip for a concert ticket to muralism, his work with Self Help Graphics & Art in East Los Angeles and the Cesar Chavez Memorial, and his role as a cultural ambassador.
ideas: Public art can invite young people to take pride in their heritage
Art bridges two cultures across a border
The mural movement as community building and social commentary
orgs: Mexican Cultural Institute of Los Angeles

episodes.title: Ash Hanson: Exclamation Points
episodes.summary: Ash Hanson, founder of PlaceBase Productions and CEO of the Department of Public Transformation, describes two decades of making original, site-specific musicals with rural Minnesota towns. She explains how place stories gathered at bingo nights, rodeos and county fairs help communities heal and find common ground, and how artists can work inside housing and planning agencies.
ideas: Place stories help communities heal and find common ground
Rural culture deserves celebration and advocacy
Play and exclamation points have real power

episodes.title: The Griot in the Prison Yard:  Provoking Community Healing Through Story
episodes.summary: Storyteller Michael McCarty, a former Black Panther, Army martial arts instructor and acupuncturist who founded the GRIOT Workshop in Los Angeles's Leimert Park, shares High John the Conqueror and other folktales. He describes teaching storytelling in prisons and his belief that every person has at least one story they need to tell.
ideas: Every living person has at least one story they need to tell
Telling that story heals relationships with others and with oneself
Folktales carry survival wisdom across generations

episodes.title: How Robert Farid Karimi Uses Food & Comedy as a Cultural Strategy for Social Change
episodes.summary: Comedian, chef, poet and educator Robert Farid Karimi, the People's Chef, explores the 'in-between': how humor and shared cooking can bridge conflict-ridden communities, the power of gossip in immigrant cultures, and what organizers can learn from Mel Brooks and Cheech and Chong.
ideas: Humor can lift a room and bridge a divided community
The fool and gossip have power in a post-truth era
Play helps people see themselves as storytellers
episodes.repriseOf: Originally episode 32 (republished under this number, per its web address)

episodes.title: How Salty Xi Jie Ng Uses Humor, Bunions, and Grandmas to Drive Art and Social Change - Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with Singapore-born artist Salty Xi Jie Ng follows her playful, personal projects: Bunion2Bunion, about inheritance and her grandmother's feet; a project with art gallery security staff; and a comedy show with incarcerated artists. She questions who artists are and what gets called art.
ideas: Deeply personal work can open broad questions about inheritance
Invisible workers in art institutions have their own expertise
Humor and play as tools for care and subversion
episodes.repriseOf: Originally episode 37 (republished under this number, per its web address)

episodes.title: Salty: Activist Artists and Cultural Organizers Changing the World Through Art - Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one with Salty Xi Jie Ng, a Singapore-born 'citizen scholar of the cosmos' whose genre-defying projects might be a film, a feast, a newspaper or a party. She talks about growing up in Singapore, grandmothers and intimacy, the global Grandma Reporter newspaper, and The Inside Show made with incarcerated artists.
ideas: Everyday life as performance
Questioning who artists are and what gets called art
Inviting audiences to choose whether to watch or take part
episodes.repriseOf: Originally episode 36 (republished under this number, per its web address)

episodes.title: TRICKSTER SERIES: Bonus Episode: Normando Performs
episodes.summary: A bonus episode of performances by Normando Ismay: his adaptation of the traditional South American story Cachiru, with his own accompaniment on quena and bombo, and Magdelina and Jose, a love story set during Argentina's Dirty War, written and performed with Mike O'Dowd.
ideas: Traditional South American stories told with music
Remembering the disappeared of Argentina's Dirty War
Love story as a lens on state terror

episodes.title: TRICKSTER SERIES: From Crack Houses to Trickster Tales: Normando Ismay is Thriving as an Artist for Change
episodes.summary: Argentine-born painter, poet, storyteller and performance artist Normando Ismay, 'a serious trickster shapeshifter,' talks with Bill about his traveling performance spaces and installations, from Little Beirut and Cafe Bizzoso in Atlanta to Chilicito, a town he built inside a Swedish museum for Chilean exiles. The conversation moves through magical realism, cultural appropriation and Atlanta's crack epidemic.
ideas: Intimate, site-specific venues bring storyteller and audience close
Art can make statements about exile and cultural appropriation
The trickster as a creative and survival stance
orgs: City of Atlanta Bureau of Cultural Affairs
episodes.repriseOf: Originally episode 28 (republished under this number, per its web address)

episodes.title: Pills Alone Won’t Heal Us!  The Case for Art and Social Change in Healthcare
episodes.summary: Researchers Jill Sonke (University of Florida Center for Arts in Medicine) and Tasha Golden (International Arts + Mind Lab, Johns Hopkins) introduce 'Arts on Prescription: A Field Guide for US Communities.' They explain social prescribing, where health providers refer patients to arts, culture and nature, drawing on Massachusetts' CultureRX pilots and research from other countries.
ideas: Health is generated in communities, not only in clinics
Arts on prescription looks different in every community, and that is a strength
A growing body of research links arts participation to mental health and lower care costs
approaches: Arts in health and arts on prescription
orgs: University of Florida Center for Arts in Medicine
International Arts + Mind Lab at Johns Hopkins Medicine
Horizon Blue Cross Blue Shield of New Jersey

episodes.title: BIGhART – BIGsTORY: Skateboarding, Storytelling, & Environmental Justice – How Artist Activists Are Thriving and Driving Social Change – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two of BIGhART BIGsTORY opens with the sound of skateboarders in Tasmania and follows Scott Rankin's Big hART into skate culture, the Namatjira Project and environmental justice. Rankin explains that 80 percent of the work is process, and the real work is breaking down permissions about who gets to be a maker.
ideas: Make invisible stories visible
Process and who is welcomed into it matter more than content
Skate culture as an emerging art form for young people

episodes.title: BIGhART – BIGsTORY: Skateboarding, Storytelling, & Environmental Justice – How Artist Activists Are Thriving and Driving Social Change
episodes.summary: Part one of BIGhART BIGsTORY. Scott Rankin describes how Big hART grew over 30 years into one of the world's leading arts and social change organizations. The episode opens at the 2006 Melbourne International Arts Festival premiere of Ngapartji Ngapartji, Trevor Jamieson's story of the Maralinga atomic tests and the Spinifex people, told in Pitjantjatjara and English.
ideas: Authentic, high-quality art made with communities
Everyone, everywhere has the right to thrive
Positive generational change begins as a cultural shift

episodes.title: Tisidra Jones: Strong and Starlike
episodes.summary: Tisidra Jones, an artist trained in theater and music who is also a lawyer, describes her company, Strong and Starlike Consulting, which blends legal and policy research, sociology and arts-based civic engagement to help organizations navigate systems. She talks about cross-sector, hybrid leadership, Dred and Harriet Scott Days at Historic Fort Snelling, and the Creative Community Leadership Institute.
ideas: Cross-sector, hybrid creative leadership
People who navigate a system should help design it
Art helps translate across organizational and community cultures
orgs: University of St. Thomas School of Law
Center for the Study of Art & Community

episodes.title: Henry’s Return: Further Adventures of an Activist Artist from San Quentin
episodes.summary: A follow-up with Henry Frank, a Yurok and Pomo artist and former lifer at San Quentin, two years after his first appearance. He shares new chapters of his journey, including a gifted grizzly bear pelt tied to his people's bear healing traditions, ceremonies, and his work as a teaching artist in California prisons with the William James Association.
ideas: Art gives voice to Native and incarcerated people beyond reservations and prison walls
Healing traditions and ceremony sustain life after prison
Podcast stories are chapters in a continuing journey
orgs: AKTA Lakota Museum and Cultural Center

episodes.title: A Radical Mama: The Art and Power of Amoke Kubat’s Cultural Resistance
episodes.summary: Àmọ̀kẹ́ Kubat of North Minneapolis, described as an organizer, puppeteer, healer, priestess, playwright, writer, teacher, storyteller and provocateur, talks about her journey from early childhood educator to founder of Yo Mama's House, a cooperative for women who are artists, mothers, activists and healers, and her art as cultural resistance.
ideas: Hybrid, cross-sector lives rise from community needs
Art can speak truth to power and hold a position of wellness
Reclaiming Indigenous African sensibilities

episodes.title: Barry Gillespie on Art, Joy, and Compassion as Tools for Social Change and Healing
episodes.summary: Painter and meditation teacher Barry Gillespie, an old friend of Bill's from the 1970s, talks about his parallel paths of Buddhist practice and painting, from abstract geometrics to Buddhas to women weightlifters. They explore compassion, loving-kindness and empathetic joy as tools for social change and healing in dark times.
ideas: Art making and spiritual practice grew from the same seeds
Compassion and joy have a place even in terrible times
The four Brahmaviharas as a practice for change makers

episodes.title: The Book of Judith: Prison Truth Through Fiction
episodes.summary: An excerpt from The Book of Judith (New Village Press), an homage to poet and teaching artist Judith Tannenbaum. Bill and a cast dramatize how Tannenbaum wrote North Coast Correctional Facility, a fictional prison novella that changed how California's Arts in Corrections program trained outside artists to work inside prisons.
ideas: Fiction can reveal truths that rule books miss
Preparing artists for the upside-down reality of prison
Judith Tannenbaum's legacy with incarcerated writers

episodes.title: Art for Art’s Sake – NOT!—and What Activist Artist Alice Lovelace Built Instead
episodes.summary: Poet, performer and cultural organizer Alice Lovelace returns to describe her next chapter: building a multidisciplinary, cross-sector cultural institution that grew out of the pandemic in East Point, Georgia, from the legacy of the ArtsXchange she co-founded 40 years ago. The story carries lessons about foresight, ownership, accountability and history.
ideas: Owning space gives community arts organizations staying power
History is essential to building what comes next
A new cultural beachhead rising from the pandemic
orgs: Atlanta Partnership for Arts in Learning
Southern Collective of African American Writers

episodes.title: Harry Boyte: Democracy & Imagination
episodes.summary: Activist, organizer, educator and author Harry Boyte, a former field secretary for the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, explores how democracy can be an everyday practice for everyone. He discusses free spaces, the SCLC Citizenship Schools, the role of culture in the labor and civil rights movements, public work and the dignity of labor, and the inseparability of imagination and democracy.
