ideas: Nobody in the movement thought democracy was mainly elections
America is a commonwealth built through the labors of us all
Imagination and democracy are inseparable
orgs: Sabo Center for Democracy and Citizenship

episodes.title: Carlton Turner: SIPP Culture Rising -Reprise-
episodes.summary: A reprise of episode 47 with a new introduction. Carlton Turner, co-founder of the Mississippi Center for Cultural Production (Sipp Culture), describes using food and story to rebuild his hometown of Utica, Mississippi, a farming community that became a food desert. He traces his path from hip-hop and the Algebra Project with Bob Moses through leading Alternate ROOTS, and explains culture bearers and redefining wealth.
ideas: Culture is a community's whole way of life, and art grows out of it
Community work must stay accountable to the community it claims to serve
Generational change takes about 20 years, and starts by mapping where a community is

episodes.title: How a Dancing Theologian Turned Improvisation into a Global Movement for Art, Healing, and Social Change
episodes.summary: Dancer and theologian Cynthia Winton-Henry, who co-founded InterPlay with Phil Porter in 1989, describes how an improvisational practice of movement, story, stillness and voice grew into a worldwide community for art, healing and social change. She talks about body wisdom, earth-based spirituality and the dance pioneers who shaped her.
ideas: The body is the starting point for wisdom
Reconvening the ancient circle of dance, song and story
Improvisation can build community and health

episodes.title: Alice Lovelace: How to Thrive as an Activist Artist and Creative Change Agent
episodes.summary: A reprise of Bill's 2021 conversation with poet, performer and cultural organizer Alice Lovelace, a 'peaceful disrupter' who brought poetry to young writers across the rural South and returned to help Atlanta's ArtsXchange through the pandemic. It opens with a roll call of current ArtsXchange programs.
ideas: A peaceful disrupter shifts power without getting loud
Teaching artists should ask students' permission to be there
Don't feed a false narrative by responding to it

episodes.title: Brain Dance: How the Arts Rewire Us for Justice and Belonging (Cultural Organizing + Neuroscience Connect)
episodes.summary: After two episodes on Breaking Ice, Bill shares his letter to the company about what neuroscience can teach about our struggle with difference: flow, the importance of stories and play in human development, and how the brain processes in-groups and out-groups. He stresses that anti-racism takes moral courage, not science projects.
ideas: Brain science can help explain our struggle with difference
Stories and play are central to human development
Equitable community-making is a multi-generational moral quest

episodes.title: When Fear Meets Hope:  Theater and Dialogue in Healthcare DEI (Arts Activism + Cultural Organizing) – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two of the Breaking Ice story. Five Breaking Ice performers on a bare stage at Barnes Jewish Hospital in St. Louis in 2019 explore fear of judgment, guilt, humility and responsibility before about 300 hospital staff, breaking the fourth wall to share their own fears. Company members Noël Raymond and Kurt Kwan discuss the work.
ideas: Name what you're afraid of
Not knowing is not an excuse for hurtful actions
Theater lets audiences recognize their own hopes and fears

episodes.title: When Fear Meets Hope:  Theater and Dialogue in Healthcare DEI (Arts Activism + Cultural Organizing) – Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one of Bill's time with Breaking Ice, the theater-based diversity, equity and inclusion program of Pillsbury House + Theatre in Minneapolis, as five actors perform for about 200 staff at Barnes Jewish Hospital in St. Louis. Bill traces the program's evolution, history, impact and its approach to cultivating courageous dialogue in workplaces.
ideas: Theater can cultivate courageous dialogue about difference
Scenes of everyday workplace blunders let audiences see themselves
Health disparities and stigma shape the workplace

episodes.title: A Culture of Care: Art, Neuroscience, and Belonging in Aging Communities – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with Dominic Campbell explores the roles artists can play at the intersection of science, healthcare and policymaking, the conditions that support radical collaborative thinking, and how artists help scientists move from 'lab to table.' He describes being in the first cohort of Atlantic Fellows at the Global Brain Health Institute and its turn toward the social determinants of health.
ideas: The vehicle that got you this far may not get you to the next bit
Artists help scientists communicate with the real world
Equity and the culture of healthcare matter for brain health
orgs: Atlantic Fellows for Equity in Brain Health

episodes.title: Is Creative Aging the Cutting Edge of Community Arts?
episodes.summary: International arts and aging leader Dominic Campbell, former director of Ireland's Bealtaine Festival and of St. Patrick's Festival, asks whether an active creative culture can change the scary stories we tell about getting older. He talks about Caribbean Carnival, large-scale festivals as common ground, and why creative aging is being embraced by gerontologists and brain scientists.
ideas: Creating the culture from which ideas emerge
Festivals can help communities meet the challenges of an aging population
Creative aging is gaining ground with public health and brain science
places: Port of Spain, Trinidad and Tobago

episodes.title: An Activist Artist at Work at the Global Brain Health Institute
episodes.summary: Mexico City-born painter Veronica Rojas, an Atlantic Fellow at the Global Brain Health Institute at UCSF, talks about advancing creative aging alongside neurologists, architects, economists and other artists. She describes working with artists with disabilities and neurocognitive disorders and why arts and medicine are finding common ground in dementia care.
ideas: Collective challenges demand collective understanding and solutions
Learning from artists with disabilities and neurocognitive disorders
Arts and medicine share common ground in dementia care
approaches: Arts in health and arts on prescription
orgs: Memory and Aging Center at UCSF

episodes.title: Anne Basting -Aging, Arts and Social Change: A Radical Prescription
episodes.summary: MacArthur Fellow Anne Basting, founder of TimeSlips and professor at the University of Wisconsin Milwaukee, explains how creative aging became a powerful prescription for reducing isolation, promoting social connection and easing dementia symptoms. She discusses reinvigorating people's capacity for creativity, the Penelope Project, Peter Pan with 12 rural Kentucky nursing homes, and memory cafes.
ideas: Creative expression should extend from childhood through late life
Invite people to access their creativity, then help shape and direct it
Creative engagement belongs in every aging care system
approaches: Arts in health and arts on prescription

episodes.title: Roadside Theater’s 50-Year Legacy Is a Blueprint for Democracy Through the Arts and Cultural Organizing
episodes.summary: Editor Ben Fink and contributor Arnaldo J. López discuss Art in a Democracy: Selected Plays of Roadside Theater, two volumes covering 50 years of Appalshop's Roadside Theater in Whitesburg, Kentucky. Songs and tall tales from the coal fields of Eastern Kentucky spread to collaborations with Junebug Productions, Pregones in the Bronx and the Zuni Pueblo, and into the prison system.
ideas: A 50-year blueprint for democracy through the arts
Cross-cultural theater collaborations between communities
Stories from the coal fields that travel across America

episodes.title: Eric Booth: From Shakespeare on Broadway to Pioneering Teaching Artist Organizer
episodes.summary: Former Broadway actor Eric Booth, the first artist to receive the nation's highest award in arts education, describes 45 years of pioneering work building the teaching artist field. He talks about activating the artistry of others to foster wellness, thriving communities and behavior change, El Sistema and music for social change, and founding the International Teaching Artist Collaborative.
ideas: Activating the artistry of others
Teaching artists as a field built over 45 years
Flow and humbling experiences as pathways to purpose

episodes.title: Arlene Goldbard on Cultural Activism, Belonging, and the Power of Lived Knowledge
episodes.summary: Writer, visual artist and cultural activist Arlene Goldbard discusses her book In the Camp of Angels of Freedom: What Does It Mean to Be Educated?, which traces her life alongside 11 'angels' including James Baldwin, Nina Simone, Paulo Freire, Doris Lessing and Jane Jacobs. The conversation covers credentialism, false dichotomies, the evil of indifference and an art-fueled vision of possibility.
ideas: Little stories of our lives open into the big story crying to be told
The tyranny of credentialism and false dichotomies
Lived knowledge as real education
orgs: US Department of Arts and Culture

episodes.title: Lorrie Chang - Finding an Art & Community TRUE NORTH
episodes.summary: Researcher, writer and planner Lorrie Chang revisits her work as PolicyLink's research partner for ArtPlace America's Community Development Investments program, including the Southwest Minnesota Housing Partnership's Partnership Art and the Zuni Youth Empowerment Project. She reflects on integrating arts into community development and her own journey toward personal and collective liberation.
ideas: Community developers can make arts-based tools an enduring core of practice
Storytelling-rooted engagement for a thriving Black community
Personal liberation in service of collective liberation
orgs: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts

episodes.title: Witches Are Not Victims: Liz Lerman on Power, Performance & Cultural Legacy – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with choreographer Liz Lerman focuses on Wicked Bodies, her work exploring the ugly, beautiful and sublime in the age-old story of witches, presented at the Yerba Buena Center for the Arts. She traces its origins to a museum exhibit in Edinburgh and discusses authority, the criminalizing of difference, and Christine Blasey Ford.
ideas: Witches are not victims
Authority's impulse to criminalize difference
Every witch has a story
orgs: Yerba Buena Center for the Arts

episodes.title: Witches Are Not Victims: Liz Lerman on Power, Performance & Cultural Legacy – Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one with choreographer Liz Lerman covers her early years, her career as a 'heretic,' the Critical Response Process, the Heisenberg Uncertainty principle, the power of the horizontal, and how dance can make the world a better place. Speaking from the Southwest, she reflects on dance as a tributary to the larger idea of motion.
ideas: Dance is a tributary to the larger idea that the world is in motion
Opening the creative process to everyone, from shipbuilders to physicists
Critique is creative
orgs: California State Summer School for the Arts

episodes.title: Change the Story- Genesis
episodes.summary: A replay of the very first Change the Story / Change the World episode, in which Bill tells the personal story of how the show came to be: a troubled home, drugs, rock and roll, the National Cathedral choir, hippie communes and a geodesic dome, then CETA, artist colonies in California prisons and the growth of the global community arts movement.
ideas: The creative process can be a lifeline for people who are struggling
CETA gave birth to an expanding community arts movement
Artists must build trust with new communities and partners
approaches: Artists in public service (CETA and its successors)
orgs: Center for the Study of Art & Community

episodes.title: What 2022 Taught Us About Thriving as Artists for Change
episodes.summary: A year-end episode in which Bill answers four listener questions from 2022: how to build creative partnerships in prison (using a baseball metaphor about why early projects struck out), teaching the arts online, the 'Tyranny of Comfort,' and what neuroscience can tell us about arts and change.
ideas: Understand why you keep striking out before blaming a rigged game
Comfort can block change
Neuroscience offers insight into arts and change

episodes.title: Rad Pereira on Ancestry, Imagination & Liberation (Art and Social Change in Practice)
episodes.summary: Theater artist, writer, educator and community activist Rad Pereira, a multi-spirit mixed Black, Indigenous Brazilian and Jewish (im)migrant artist based in Brooklyn, asks how we can imagine and manifest alternate futures together. They talk about healing justice, Afro-futurism, Occupy Wall Street, Theatre of the Oppressed, and work as an NYC public artist in residence with LGBTQIA foster youth.
ideas: Healing justice: spaces safe enough to imagine healing-centered stories
Afro-futurism invites alternate timelines and liberation
Can the natural world function as a moral compass?

episodes.title: Barry Marcus Redux- A Creative Culture Celebratory Remembrance
episodes.summary: Grieving the loss of his friend Barry Marcus, songwriter, therapist and director of children's mental health programs, Bill replays Barry's 2020 Change the Story conversation as a celebratory remembrance. Barry describes turning residential care at the Sacramento Children's Home and Families First into communities of creativity, including 'Our Stuff, Our Song,' where children wrote and performed their own songs.
ideas: Treat each child as a guest, not a list of deficits
Institutions can become communities of creativity
Performance as ritual and rite of passage for young people

episodes.title: Susie Tanner: When Steelworkers Became Activist Artists— And What It Taught Us About Dignity, Loss, and Change – Part 2
episodes.summary: The second chapter of the TheatreWorkers Project story. After Episode 59's account of Susie Tanner, Bruce Springsteen and a band of unemployed steelworkers touring Lady Beth across America, Susie works with incarcerated and formerly incarcerated artists who share their stories. (Tagged from the short show notes only; no transcript was available.)
ideas: Theater built from workers' and prisoners' own stories
Carrying the TheatreWorkers model from steel towns to prisons
Formerly incarcerated artists telling their stories

episodes.title: Susie Tanner: When Steelworkers Became Activist Artists— And What It Taught Us About Dignity, Loss, and Change – Part 1
episodes.summary: Theater director Susie Tanner tells how she founded TheatreWorkers Project in 1983 with laid-off steelworkers from the Bethlehem Steel mill in Vernon, California. Their workshops became 'Lady Beth: The Steelworkers' Play,' which Bruce Springsteen helped take on a 16-city tour of towns where steel mills had closed.
ideas: Working people's own stories can carry great poetry and drama
Making a play together became a way to grieve a lost mill and livelihood
Community-made work should be as polished as any professional production

episodes.title: Why Rural Stories Get Erased—And What Activist Artist Organizers Like Matthew Fluharty Are Doing to Stop It – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with Matthew Fluharty of Art of the Rural continues the story of Sauget, Illinois, and explores the power of nostalgia, the iconic status of Busch Light beer and the legacy of Family Video. He contrasts the yearning voice of home place and land with the heroic myth of loss and resentment, and describes the High Visibility collaboration with the Plains Art Museum.
ideas: Dueling American stories about the pastoral past
Everyday rural culture doesn't need decorating to matter
What parts of our stories connect and can be honored?

episodes.title: Why Rural Stories Get Erased—And What Activist Artist Organizers Like Matthew Fluharty Are Doing to Stop It – Part 1
episodes.summary: Matthew Fluharty, poet, essayist, curator and founder of Art of the Rural, talks about reframing the prevailing narrative of rural America and Indian Country through High Visibility with the Plains Art Museum, and the American Bottom Project in the floodplain of the East St. Louis region, where Cahokia Mounds abuts a Superfund site. Bill recalls the Perpich Center artist-educator gatherings in Winona.
ideas: Rural stories get erased by prevailing narratives
Multigenerational knowledge teaches where we've been and might go
A fractured landscape holds layered histories
orgs: Andy Warhol Foundation for the Visual Arts

episodes.title: Lorraine Hansberry @ Pillsbury House + Theatre - Gifted & Black
episodes.summary: A bonus audio portrait of To Sit a While, a project at Pillsbury House + Theatre celebrating playwright, journalist and activist Lorraine Hansberry, whose A Raisin in the Sun was the first play by a Black woman produced on Broadway. It is part of the Lorraine Hansberry Initiative from The Lillys, which uses public art and artist scholarships to honor her legacy. The episode opens with a song by Twin Cities artist Frida Ross.
ideas: Hansberry laid bare systemic racism in the American dreamscape
Her legacy for Black and LGBTQ communities endures
Public art and scholarships invest in those following in her footsteps

episodes.title: How a Minneapolis Social Service Agency Became A Center for Art and Social Change – Part 2
episodes.summary: The second chapter of the Pillsbury House + Theatre story. At the corner of George Floyd Square and the pandemic, artistic producing director Signe Harriday and co-artistic managing director Noël Raymond describe how the pandemic and George Floyd's murder affected the arts-based community development agency and its neighborhood, and how they are shaping what comes next.
ideas: Arts and culture can stimulate community health, ownership and justice
The pandemic erased the small spontaneous moments that build community
Who are my people and where can I be safe?

episodes.title: How a Minneapolis Social Service Agency Became A Center for Art and Social Change – Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one of the Pillsbury House + Theatre story. Bill imagines the prehistoric artist-healer at the center of the tribe, then introduces Pillsbury House + Theatre in Minneapolis, a full-time creative community center serving 30,000 people where social workers, teachers, health workers and community artists work side by side. Signe Harriday and Noël Raymond describe its culturally infused practice.
ideas: A new model for human service work built on arts and culture
Artists as full partners in building the beloved community
Not a pilot but a long-running creative community center

episodes.title: The Nouvella – Using Fiction to Tell the Truth About Art and Social Change
episodes.summary: A bonus replay of Bill's presentation to the 16th Annual Art in Society Conference in June 2021 on story-based strategies for community arts training. It includes a made-up game show called Truth or No, a scene from Judith Tannenbaum's novella about artists working in a fictional prison, and a visit to a fictional town in the midst of a reckoning over race, justice, othering and belonging.
ideas: Fiction can tell the truth about art and social change
Stories help prepare artists for work in communities and institutions
Judith Tannenbaum's lessons on art making and imagination
orgs: Center for the Study of Art & Community

episodes.title: DAH Teatar: Arts Driven Social Change and Environmental Justice in Serbia
episodes.summary: Director Dijana Milošević, co-founder of DAH Teatar Research Center in Belgrade, and Bill recall the company's birth on the eve of the Yugoslav wars and its dangerous 1992 street performance challenging the government's denial of the war in Bosnia. They discuss decades of theater for peacebuilding and feminist activism, and recent work on environmental justice and Rio Tinto's mining plans in Serbia.
ideas: Oppose destruction and violence with the creation of meaning
A third theater born of relationships within the company and community
Bold art can provoke personal and social transformation
orgs: DAH Teatar Research Center for Culture and Social Change

episodes.title: Garden Battles and River Rituals: How Felicia Young Heals Communities with Art and Activism
episodes.summary: Social action artist Felicia Young, founder of Earth Celebrations, describes using arts-based strategies to spur community action: a 15-year pageant campaign that helped save hundreds of New York community gardens, Hudson River restoration, an international effort to restore the Vaigai River in Madurai, India, and climate solutions on Manhattan's Lower East Side. Her path began as a youth intern at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.
ideas: Art objects were once part of socially functional ritual
Why should art be relegated to producing for the marketplace?
Pageants and ritual can build coalitions for ecological change

episodes.title: Bonus Reprise: Jan Cohen Cruz - Meeting the Moment
episodes.summary: A bonus replay of the November 2021 conversation with Jan Cohen-Cruz, marking the publication of Meeting the Moment: Socially Engaged Performance, 1965-2020, written with Rad Pereira. She recounts her path as an actor, activist and teacher, from street theater in Trenton State Prison to NYU and Imagining America, and her role chronicling socially engaged performance.
ideas: Learning with students, not from a teacher
Chronicling the history of socially engaged performance
Art does far more in the world than many imagine

episodes.title: From Clowning to PBS: An Activist Artist’s Journey Through Media and Justice
episodes.summary: Filmmaker Gary Glassman traces his path from clowning, fire-eating, stilt walking and street theater to participatory media projects with prisoners, hospitalized children and developmentally disabled adults, and then to Emmy-winning documentaries for PBS and other broadcasters, including the series Native America. Bill recalls the circus arts program at San Quentin through Arts in Corrections.
ideas: Storytelling is the foundation; film is the medium
Television can change the world
Circus and street performance as a path to media

episodes.title: Subito Story 1: Karina Kantas
episodes.summary: The first Subito Story, a short feature: Bill visits author Karina Kantas on the Greek island of Corfu, where she has lived for 28 years. Inspired by S.E. Hinton's The Outsiders, she began writing rebel fiction and found that writing helped her acknowledge and heal a long-ignored trauma.
ideas: Imagination is the most powerful aspect of being human
A kindred-spirit book can launch a creative life
There is always a piece of the author in her books
orgs: Center for the Study of Art & Community

episodes.title: Wayne Cook - A Dream Recalled
episodes.summary: Wayne Cook, who calls himself 'bumpy,' tells a life story of abrupt changes: promising young athlete, crash victim, soldier in Germany, child therapist, stage actor, 'the Black Mr. Rogers,' 23 years at the California Arts Council, author of a drama curriculum, and performer of Langston Hughes. He describes the arts as both through-line and lifeline.
ideas: How you deal with failure decides whether it defeats or inspires you
The flexibility learned in the arts helps maneuver life's bumps
Children's play as the start of theater

episodes.title: From Combat Zone to Camera Lens: A Veteran Artist’s Journey to Reclaim His War Story
episodes.summary: Vietnam veteran David Moragne returned to Vietnam with his comrades in 2001 to ask when a war truly ends. His film Flashback: Summer Sail One Revisited documents what they discovered. Bill frames the story with South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission and America's failure to reconcile with the Vietnam War.
ideas: When does a war truly end?
Veterans seeking their own reconciliation with history
Film as a way to reclaim a war story

episodes.title: Art & Upheaval: Activist Artists on the World’s Frontline
episodes.summary: Bill revisits stories from his book Art and Upheaval: Artists on the World's Frontlines, set to his song of the same name, to argue that creativity can help vanquish the forces of evil. Stories range from DAH Teatar in Milosevic's Serbia and post-Khmer Rouge Cambodia to South Africa and the Watts Writers Workshop in Los Angeles.
ideas: Some think you can't beat the devil with a song, but they don't know
Art on the frontlines of war, terror and repression
Exercising the imaginative muscles
orgs: Reyum Institute of Arts and Culture

episodes.title: Why Listening — Not Loud Ideas — Should Lead Your Art and Social Change Practice
episodes.summary: London-based American artist Jennifer Williams, founder of the British American Arts Association and the Centre for Creative Communities, talks about being a 'joined up' connector: writer, policymaker, provocateur and maker of hand-made books and etchings. She and Bill discuss small stories from out-of-the-way places, puppets and people, the sanctity of tools, and policy change linked to creative, collaborative convenings.
ideas: Small stories from out-of-the-way places can make a big difference
Convenings that walk the talk can provoke policy change
Humans are makers and collaborators

episodes.title: SIPP Culture Rising: How A Small Southern Town Is Becoming a National Model for Cultural Organizing
episodes.summary: Artist, agriculturalist and researcher Carlton Turner, co-founder of the Mississippi Center for Cultural Production (Sipp Culture), describes using food and story to support rural community development in Utica, Mississippi, where his family has lived for eight generations. He talks about comprehensive community cultural development, the civil rights legacy of Bob Moses and SNCC, Alternate ROOTS, and his performance group M.U.G.A.B.E.E.
ideas: When you can't feed yourself, the imagination is the first thing to go
The exponential power of the hyper-local
Centering culture and the people's history in community development

episodes.title: Elise Witt - All Singing: How One Artist’s Songs Became a Passport to Learning, Connection, and Thriving
episodes.summary: Singer, songwriter, song leader and community activist Elise Witt, born in Switzerland and based in Pine Lake, Georgia, sings in more than a dozen languages and has served as a cultural ambassador to South Africa, Nicaragua, China, Italy and Yugoslavia. She talks about her songbook All Singing, a daily antidote of song on Zoom, Alternate ROOTS, the Global Village Project, and songs as a passport to connection.
ideas: Song as a daily antidote and passport to connection
Music and languages as tools for cultural exchange
Community song leading builds belonging

episodes.title: Why Ron Chew Believes Museums Should Be Cultural Centers, Not Just Store Artifacts
episodes.summary: Journalist, museum director and healthcare executive Ron Chew, a quiet 'story whisperer,' describes a life telling hidden stories of Seattle's Asian Pacific Islander community. He discusses growing up with whispered family stories from the era of Chinese exclusion, the International Examiner, and transforming the Wing Luke Museum into a community-driven cultural center.
ideas: A museum can be a force for social change
History can heal and stories can be unforgotten
Museums should be cultural centers, not just storehouses

episodes.title: How an Hollywood Director/ Artivist Used Film to Fight Censorship, Racism, & Fear – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with film and television director Jeremy Kagan focuses on trust in social impact art making and his film Crown Heights, about the 1991 violence between Black and Orthodox Jewish communities in Brooklyn and two young men who found common ground through hip hop. They discuss the open ending, Aaron Zigman's score, and how art acts as a trust bridge and translator.
ideas: Audiences trust the storyteller with their hearts and minds
Art as trust bridge and translator across conflict
Hard stories need open endings

episodes.title: How a Hollywood Director/Artivist Used Film to Fight Censorship, Racism, & Fear – Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one with film and television director Jeremy Kagan, whose career shows that story on the big, small and community screen can entertain and change hearts and minds. The episode opens with the Hays Code and Kagan's ACLU series The Freedom Files on free speech, voting rights and racial profiling, then turns to his work founding the USC Change-making Media Lab and the 'imagination business.'
ideas: Stories are what distinguish us: recreating past and future
Entertainment-education can change behavior
Film as a tool against censorship and fear

episodes.title: How Pangea World Theater Became a Cultural Organizing Force After George Floyd’s Murder – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with Meena Natarajan and Dipankar Mukherjee of Pangea World Theater asks how a small community-based cultural institution can keep the power and integrity of its healing and community building amid chaos. They discuss artists as stewards and healers, displacement on Lake Street after the fires, climate injustice, close ties with neighbors and businesses, and reimagining language.
ideas: Artists must take responsibility for the time they live in
Healing and rebuilding must be intersectional
The Tower of Babel is a tower of many languages and truths
orgs: National Institute for Directing and Ensemble Creation

episodes.title: How Pangea World Theater Became a Cultural Organizing Force After George Floyd’s Murder – Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one with Pangea World Theater's Meena Natarajan and Dipankar Mukherjee, whose 25th anniversary year was spent helping their Minneapolis community heal after the murder of George Floyd. They describe Pangea's 'total theater' rooted in Indian traditions, its relational, process-centered way of working across differences, and artists stepping up on the front lines to document, listen and organize.
ideas: When a community is burning, artists step up to document, listen and create
Process is as important as product
Theater that includes music, dance and visual art

episodes.title: A Loving Trickster: Using Culture, Story, and Disruption to Spark Art & Social Change
episodes.summary: A between-seasons reprise of the popular conversation with Normando Ismay, 'the Loving Trickster.' The Argentine-born painter, storyteller and performance installation artist introduces the 'Bizzoso Universe' of Atlanta venues like Little Beirut and Cafe Bizzoso, Chilicito in Sweden, and characters including Contralabias the smuggler and the Last Inca.
ideas: Intimate, site-specific venues bring storyteller and audience close
Art can make statements about exile and cultural appropriation
The trickster as a creative stance
orgs: Center for the Study of Art & Community

episodes.title: Beth Thielen: LOVE AND FREEDOM: Our Most Imaginative Activist Artists Are Locked in Prison
episodes.summary: A reprise of the season-one conversation with book artist Beth Thielen, who has made artist books with incarcerated people since her first class at the California Institution for Women in 1985. She describes teaching at San Quentin and in girls' group homes, and the question that drives her work: what relationship does love have to freedom?
ideas: Art can begin with a question, like what love has to do with freedom
Teaching is a way to make work with people rather than about them
People surviving prison bring great imagination to scarcity
episodes.repriseOf: 4 (originally released as episode 4; republished under this number, per its web address)

episodes.title: Gallery to Garden: Beverly Naidus on Art, Activism, and Reimagining the Future
episodes.summary: Artist, educator and community healer Beverly Naidus, whose participatory installations and artist books have addressed unemployment, nuclear fear, body hate, consumerism and the climate emergency, talks about art for social change and healing. She describes her installation inviting visitors to imagine themselves as ancestors, teaching at UW Tacoma, her book Arts for Change, and co-directing SEEDS.
ideas: Vulnerable storytelling generates others' stories and can catalyze action
Grief and gratitude weave together in the climate emergency
Imagine yourself as an ancestor to future generations
orgs: SEEDS (Social Ecology Education and Demonstration School)

episodes.title: Meeting the Moment: How 67 Activist Artists Changed the Story of American Theater
episodes.summary: Writer, educator and former actor Jan Cohen-Cruz, former director of Imagining America and longtime NYU professor of applied theatre, talks about her path from street theater workshops in Trenton State Prison to chronicling socially engaged performance, and about Meeting the Moment: Socially Engaged Theater, 1965 to 2020, written with Rad Pereira.
ideas: Learning with students, not from a teacher
Chronicling what art is doing in the world
Art lets us connect with people in every situation

episodes.title: From Life in Prison to Life as a Cultural Leader: The Redemption of Henry Frank
episodes.summary: Henry Frank, a former gang member serving 29 years to life at San Quentin, describes how he refused to die in prison and began a journey of introspection through the arts, education and self-help. Painting led him back to his Yurok and Pomo culture, language and ceremony; a mentor showed him true friendship; and he became a respected artist, educator and cultural leader.
ideas: None of us are trash; none of us are unredeemable
Art opened a path back to culture and heritage
Don't go in to save or judge people

episodes.title: Why Artist and Cultural Organizers in Hospitals Are Changing How We Heal
episodes.summary: Dancer, educator and researcher Jill Sonke, director of the University of Florida Center for Arts in Medicine and senior advisor to the CDC COVID-19 vaccine confidence team, describes the 30-year history of UF's Arts in Medicine program and its artists in residence at Shands Hospital. She discusses arts in public health, research, and reuniting the arts and medicine as healing partners.
ideas: Arts and medicine as age-old healing partners
Artists in residence transform the culture of care
Arts can help public health communication
approaches: Arts in health and arts on prescription
orgs: University of Florida Center for Arts in Medicine
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

episodes.title: Joe Lambert - Making Good Stories that Help Us
episodes.summary: Joe Lambert, director of StoryCenter in Berkeley, talks about the history, practice and influence of digital storytelling, opening with 'The Story of My Story,' a young undocumented woman's digital story about fighting for her education and refusing to be a poster child. Lambert, who calls himself a small businessman who wants to be a revolutionary, describes his path as organizer and 'escuchador' (listener).
ideas: We all have stories that can inspire, teach and bear witness
Making good stories that help us
The storyteller must own their story

episodes.title: From Judy Chicago to Juvenile Halls: How One Activist Artist Facilitated Radical Change Through Creativity
episodes.summary: Textile artist, photographer and facilitator Susan Hill recalls her work on Judy Chicago's The Dinner Party, painting The Great Wall with Judy Baca and SPARC, and teaching in prisons and juvenile halls through Artists in Prison and Other Places. She talks about collaboration, council circles, earning the respect of people who distrust you, and what happens when the lights go off in a high-security prison classroom.
ideas: Work collaboratively for social change, large or small
Council circles give everyone an equitable voice
Earning trust from people who distrust you
orgs: Social and Public Art Resource Center (SPARC)
Artists in Prison and Other Places

episodes.title: The Music Is Her Prayer: How Becky Reardon Found Sacred Connection in Nature, Song. And Activism
episodes.summary: Singer and composer Becky Reardon, familiar to millions from the Charlie Brown TV specials, describes herself as 'in the music.' Her songs and rounds, sung by choirs and song circles in several countries, convey her passion for the natural world and the cycles of life. She talks about writing songs that carry the feelings that inspired them, a juniper tree song about aging, and asking what your community needs that you have to give.
ideas: A song should carry the feelings that inspired it
Ask what your community needs that you have to give
Reverence and awe for the natural world through song

episodes.title: The Nouvella: The Strange True Story of a Fake Prison That Trained Hundreds of Artist Activists
episodes.summary: Bill's June 2021 presentation to the online 16th Annual Art in Society Conference on story-based community arts training. It includes a game show, a scene from a novella about artists working in prison (the 'fake prison that trained hundreds of artist activists'), and a visit to a fake town in the midst of a harsh reckoning around race, justice, othering and belonging.
ideas: Stories prepare artists and partners from other sectors for work in communities
Fiction can tell the truth about institutions
Training in 'unreal time' during the pandemic

episodes.title: Why Traditional Education Fails Students—and How Activist Artists and Educators are Turning the Tide
episodes.summary: Theater artist and educator Jessa Brie Moreno, co-founder of Studio Pathways and founder of the performing arts program at Oakland Technical High School, calls herself 'a midwife of creativity.' She talks about the art of teaching as transmission of wisdom, how marginalized students shine on stage, and training educators in power analysis and reconciliation through the arts.
ideas: Holding space for the birth of others' creative thinking
Performance lets teachers see students through their assets
Educators need to do power analysis in the classroom

episodes.title: Su-lin Ngiam-An Activist Artist in Singapore is an Agent of Hope
episodes.summary: Su-Lin Ngiam, co-founder of Singapore's ArtsWok Collaborative, describes being an 'agent of hope' and an intermediary across sectors in a tightly regulated city-state. She talks about bringing taboo topics like death, inequality and the conditions of migrant workers into the open, the Both Sides Now project on end of life, and Drama Box's touring inflatable theater, Go-Li.
ideas: Artists as agents of hope who bridge difference
Making the invisible visible and the unheard heard
Activism as creative facilitation rooted in care

episodes.title: From Theater Sets To Veterans’ Healing Circles: How David O’Fallon Crafted A Life Through Cultural Organizing and Story
episodes.summary: David O'Fallon builds things: theater sets, theater companies, 12-foot puppets, art schools for teen artists and community musicians, and theater programs for veterans of Afghanistan and Vietnam. He talks about Philadelphia's Freedom Theater, the power of being in the room with another person, helping people discover their own story, and the healing power of humanities for veterans.
ideas: Actively imagine narratives that keep us together
Being in the presence of another person is a powerful technology
Who gets to tell your story?

episodes.title: Why Activist Poet Alice Lovelace Refuses To Use the Language of Her Oppressors
episodes.summary: Poet, performer, teacher and cultural organizer Alice Lovelace, a self-described 'peaceful disrupter,' opens with her poem 'This Poem.' She talks about disrupting the status quo without getting loud, asking students' permission when she enters a classroom as a teaching artist, refusing to feed false narratives, and her work bringing poetry to young writers across the rural South.
ideas: A peaceful disrupter shifts power and the conversation
Teaching artists should ask students' permission to be there
Don't feed a false narrative by responding to it

episodes.title: Theater Isn’t Just Entertainment—It’s a Cultural Organizing Tool for Saving Democracy
episodes.summary: Theater director and educator Bob Leonard, a co-founder of Alternate ROOTS, talks about the artist's role in an uncertain world, the human passion for justice and the stories that keep our sense of direction. He describes ROOTS' participatory governance, a 200-member board still functioning after 45 years, learning the aesthetic from the audience as Roadside Theater does, and the evolution of the horse as an image of possibility. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: We understand ourselves, and justice, through our stories
Participatory rather than representative governance
Learn the aesthetic from the audience, not the commercial version

episodes.title: Justin Laing: Why Cultural Organizers Must Confront White Supremacy to Succeed
episodes.summary: Justin Laing, founder of Hillombo and former senior program officer for arts and culture at The Heinz Endowments, talks about 'taking back the land' square mile by square mile in Pittsburgh's Hill District, culture as part of liberation strategy, naming white supremacy culture inside nonprofit arts organizations, and the link between racism and capitalism. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Culture is critical to liberating minds
Name frameworks like white supremacy culture inside organizations
Racism and capitalism are intrinsically connected

episodes.title: How Oakland Culture Shaped Fantastic Negrito’s Fight for Balance and Belonging
episodes.summary: A rebroadcast of the conversation with Oakland musician Xavier Dphrepaulezz, known as Fantastic Negrito, timed to his Grammy nomination for Have You Lost Your Mind Yet. He talks about the danger of scapegoating, music and every other thing as a change agent, the need for honest talk between white and Black people, and his plans for Oakland's historic California Hotel. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Change your heart and change the world
Scapegoating is the biggest lie ever sold
White and Black people need to talk honestly to each other

episodes.title: Mary Cohen Brings Art & Social Change “Inside” & “Prisoners” & “Outsiders” Became One Choir
episodes.summary: Music educator Mary Cohen describes the Oakdale Prison Community Choir in Iowa, where incarcerated 'inside' singers and volunteer 'outside' singers have rehearsed and performed together since 2009. She explains the choir's grounding in ubuntu, its reflective writing exchanges and songwriting, and how a prison choir can serve healing and prison abolition.
ideas: Singing together is embodied connection that can turn 'them' into 'us'
Ubuntu: 'my humanity is inextricably bound with your humanity'
Music education needs more empowering ways of making music, with no wrong notes

episodes.title: Cultural Organizing in Appalachia: Building Trust, Equity, and Economic Resilience – Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with organizer Ben Fink, a self-described 'communist Jew from the Northeast,' on cultural organizing in Letcher County, Kentucky. He talks about breaking the ice by lining out shape-note hymns, the Performing Our Future coalition, turning community cooking into catering jobs for neighbors returning from incarceration, addiction and military service, and Roadside Theater's play The Future of Letcher County. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Traditional hymn singing can build trust across difference
Communities that resisted exploitation can tell their own stories and build power
Cooking versus catering: bounded imagination and job creation

episodes.title: Cultural Organizing in Appalachia: Building Trust, Equity, and Economic Resilience – Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one with organizer Ben Fink, a self-described 'communist Jew from the Northeast,' about his work with Appalshop and Performing Our Future in Eastern Kentucky: creating conditions for communities to tell their own stories, build their own power and create their own wealth, rooted in local traditions. Bill opens by inviting listeners to sing 'We who believe in freedom cannot rest.'
ideas: Forget community engagement; work with your neighbors
Making things together and owning what we make changes the story
It is hard to dehumanize someone you have built something with

episodes.title: From Mingus to Folsom: Henry Robinett on Music, Mentors, & Thriving as an Artist for Change
episodes.summary: Jazz guitarist, composer and educator Henry Robinett recalls living with his cousin Charles Mingus at Manhattan Plaza, the subsidized artist housing in New York, and how a call from artist facilitator Bill Peterson led him to teach music at Folsom Prison, where he found human beings no different from himself. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Music can help heal heads and hearts in prison
Worst expectations dissolve on contact with real people
Mentorship from a jazz legend

episodes.title: Art Is Not An Extra: Why Artist Activists & Cultural Organizers Should Be Leading Community Recovery Efforts
episodes.summary: Sharnita Johnson, arts program officer at the Geraldine R. Dodge Foundation and former Ruth Mott Foundation staffer known as the 'Queen of Community,' talks about becoming a Black woman in cultural philanthropy in Detroit, a contested public mural in Flint, Michigan that won over a skeptical commissioner, and why artists should help lead community recovery after the pandemic. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Seeing someone who looks like you opens a path
Public art can win over its fiercest critics
Creatives tell the story in ways journalism won't

episodes.title: Forget Pipe Cleaners: Why Real Cultural Organizing Is Not What You Think It Is- Part 2
episodes.summary: Part two with three leaders of the Community Arts Training (CAT) Institute at the St. Louis Regional Arts Commission: Con Christeson, Pacia Anderson and Roseann Weiss. They discuss paying artists professionally rather than doing 'pipe cleaner' crafts, working with not for communities, never clocking out, and a CAT class held while St. Louis was in turmoil after Mike Brown was killed in 2014. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Working with, not for, communities
Professional artists, paid well; not arts and crafts
Creative process as conduit, catharsis and documentation

episodes.title: Forget Pipe Cleaners: Why Real Cultural Organizing Is Not What You Think It Is – Part 1
episodes.summary: Part one with Con Christeson, Pacia Anderson and Roseann Weiss of the Community Arts Training (CAT) Institute at the St. Louis Regional Arts Commission, which Bill helped start in 1998. They describe planting seeds, listening for stories and helping people tell them, community caregiving, and the questions activist artists should ask before offering help. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Have you been invited? How do you know your help isn't harmful?
You can only teach who you are
Training as a bridge connecting people

episodes.title: STORY story
episodes.summary: Bill tells the story of Story story, a prose poem and film exploring the evolution of story as an essential part of human development. It began in 2005 during a Rockefeller Foundation residency at Bellagio on Lake Como, where Bill was writing Art and Upheaval and heard poet Wesley McNair share an unsparing poem. The episode asks where stories come from, what they do, and their power for good or ill.
ideas: Where do stories come from and what is their function?
Stories have power for good or ill
Story as an essential aspect of human development

episodes.title: Ida Oberman: Centering Love, Story, and Art for Social Change in a Public School?
episodes.summary: Ida Oberman, founder and executive director of the Community School for Creative Education, a Waldorf-inspired public charter school in Oakland's San Antonio neighborhood, talks about imagination in child development, preparing children to blaze new trails rather than win a pre-set race, parents as partners, and the power of story from kindergarten on. The episode opens with Camila Guiza-Chavez singing 'Over the Rainbow.' (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Imagination is thinking about relationships among things not yet in being
Education should build a better tomorrow, not just meet benchmarks
Sew society back together into a stronger cloth

episodes.title: How Activist Artists Like Milenko Matanovic Are Rebuilding Democracy From the Ground Up
episodes.summary: Milenko Matanovic, who grew up in former Yugoslavia, worked with the Slovenian collective Group OHO and founded the Pomegranate Center, talks about why democracy is struggling and how community art-making can teach the 'new dance' of everyday democracy. When something specific is at stake, people move from differences to contribution; artists must work with communities and set ego aside. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Everyday democracy: a staff meeting can be a kindergarten for collaboration
Specific stakes help people rise to their better selves
Artists do it with communities, not for them

episodes.title: Art Isn’t Just Decoration—Cultural Organizing is Democracy’s Secret Weapon
episodes.summary: Erik Takeshita, a fourth-generation Japanese American from St. Paul, describes 'creative people power': art and culture as a renewable power, like sun and wind, that communities can harness. Drawing on his work at the Bush Foundation, equitable philanthropy, light rail construction and sacred space, he argues that hope, agency and connection lead to collective efficacy. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Art and culture are a power that exists and must be harnessed
Hope, agency and connection lead to collective efficacy
Art is most essential when communities are struggling

episodes.title: If You’re Not Letting Struggling Kids Make Art, You’re Missing the Boat
episodes.summary: Barry Marcus, songwriter, visual storyteller, therapist and former director of children's mental health programs, recounts bringing the creative process to kids who had blown out of multiple foster homes at the Sacramento Children's Home and Families First. He describes treating each child as a guest, turning the institution into a community of creativity, and 'Our Stuff, Our Song,' which became a rite of passage. Recorded in May 2020.
ideas: Treat each child as a guest, not a list of deficits
Active art making builds ownership and agency
Performance as ritual and rite of passage

episodes.title: Sandy Agustin on Navigating the Art and Social Change Landscape (Activist Artist Spotlight)
episodes.summary: Dancer, choreographer, educator, producer and community leader Sandy Agustin, a 'creative polymath,' describes herself as a creative navigator who helps groups figure out where they want to go, what vehicle and fuel they need, and who should be in the car. She talks about asking generous, generative questions, using movement and play when groups get stuck, and growing up in Minnesota. Recorded in May 2020. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Ask generous and generative questions
Groups often already have the ruby slippers on
Move physically through space to get unstuck

episodes.title: Love at the Rivers Edge: How One Activist Artist Bridged Race & Place With Shakespeare:
episodes.summary: Actor, director, dancer, educator and anti-racism activist Kathi Bentley, recipient of the 2020 St. Louis Visionary Award, tells the story of Love at the River's Edge, a 2019 Shakespeare in the Streets production of As You Like It that brought together rural Brussels, Illinois and Pagedale, Missouri, near St. Louis. Hundreds of community members, two high schools and Beyond Housing crossed the Mississippi River to perform in each other's towns. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: People have to love each other to have each other's backs on stage
Collective creation can change settled world views
Good directing leaves community ownership behind

episodes.title: The Gunrunner for the Arts: L.O. Sloan’s Half-Century of Thriving as an Artist for Change (Part 2)
episodes.summary: Part two with Lenwood 'Leni' Sloan on the Crossroads Project in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania: winning unanimous legislative and gubernatorial support and raising funds for a monument to the demolished Eighth Ward and the struggle for the 15th and 19th Amendments. He describes monument building as community organizing and civic dialogue, its echoes of redlining and voter suppression today, and lessons on listening and humility. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: The process of making a monument can be the monument
No is a green light
Listening and humility for cultural organizers

episodes.title: The Gunrunner for the Arts: L.O. Sloan’s Half-Century of Thriving as an Artist for Change (Part 1)
episodes.summary: Part one with activist, performer, impresario and historian Lenwood O. Sloan, a 'gunrunner for the arts' whose career has unfolded like a half-century social change musical. He talks about history as an art form, African American women fighting for the vote during the 1918 flu pandemic, and creating a bold monument between the primary and the national election to call African Americans and women to vote. (Tagged from show notes; no separate transcript.)
ideas: Repositioning what already exists to create magic
History becomes art through the people in it
Monuments can reveal buried stories

episodes.title: How Art and Social Change Shaped My Life
episodes.summary: In the first episode of the podcast, then called Change the Story, Change the World (now Art is Change), Bill tells the personal story of how it came to be: a troubled home, drugs, the National Cathedral choir, hippie communes and a geodesic dome, CETA, artist colonies in prisons, the Art in Other Places conference, and armies of artists confronting Milosevic, Pol Pot and the U.S. Department of Justice.
ideas: The creative process can be a lifeline for people who are struggling
CETA gave birth to an expanding community arts movement
Artists must build trust with new communities and partners
approaches: Artists in public service (CETA and its successors)
orgs: Center for the Study of Art & Community
